meta.citation_convention: Every provision is cited as 'BNSS s.X (CrPC s.Y)'. The new code is cited first because it governs all proceedings begun after 1 July 2024; the old section number follows because many reported cases, older MCQs and bare acts still use it.

how_to_use: Read 'exam_intelligence' first: it shows where the 10 marks come from.

AIBE is open-book. Tab your Bare Act by Chapter; use the concordance table at the end to jump between CrPC and BNSS numbers quickly.

time_strategy: Most CrPC/BNSS items are recall: 60-90 seconds each. Use the open book only to confirm numbers and periods.
When the question quotes an old CrPC section, convert it using the concordance; do not guess.
For 'which of the following is NOT' questions, eliminate options that are correct under either code.
common_traps: Police custody: maximum 15 days in total (s.187), but BNSS permits it to be taken in parts within the first 40 or 60 days of the 60/90-day detention window (CrPC practice: only the first 15 days - Anupam Kulkarni).
Default bail period is 90 days only where the offence is punishable with death, life or imprisonment of not less than 10 years; 60 days for all other offences (Rakesh Kumar Paul, 2017).
Summons-case = offence NOT punishable with death, life or imprisonment exceeding 2 years; warrant-case = death, life or more than 2 years.
Anticipatory bail is not time-limited by default (Sibbia; Sushila Aggarwal); BNSS s.482(4) bars it only for BNS ss.65 and 70(2) (aggravated sexual offences against minors / gang rape of minors).
BNSS does not recognise Metropolitan Magistrates; only Sessions, JMFC, JMSC and Executive Magistrates.
FIR is not substantive evidence; s.181 (162 CrPC) statements to police cannot be signed and are used only to contradict.
Cognizance is taken of the offence, not the offender (Raghubans Dubey).
The Magistrate must examine the complainant under s.223 BNSS, and now must also hear the accused before taking cognizance on a complaint.
Section 358 (319 CrPC) needs 'strong and cogent evidence' - more than prima facie (Hardeep Singh).
Offence law is applied as at the date of the offence (Art 20(1)); procedure follows the new code for proceedings begun after 1 July 2024 (s.531).

sections.title: BNSS 2023: Overview, Transition, Definitions and Classification of Offences and Trials
sections.articles: BNSS ss.1-5 (CrPC ss.1-5); BNSS s.2 (CrPC s.2); Schedule I (classification); s.531 (repeal and savings)
sections.overview: Foundation chapter: what changed, when, and the vocabulary the rest of the paper is built on (cognizable, bailable, summons-case, warrant-case, complaint, police report, inquiry, investigation, victim).
must_know: The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Act 46 of 2023) received Presidential assent on 25 December 2023 and came into force on 1 July 2024 together with the BNS and BSA. It repeals the CrPC 1973 (s.531). The CrPC itself replaced the CrPC 1898 and came into force on 1 April 1974.

Size: BNSS has 531 sections (CrPC: 484). Hundreds of provisions were re-worded, a few dozen new provisions and many time-limits were added, and a few CrPC provisions were dropped (for example the Metropolitan Magistrate machinery and the special provision on juveniles in s.27 CrPC).

Savings (s.531(2)): appeals, applications, trials, inquiries or investigations pending on 1 July 2024 continue under the CrPC as if the BNSS had not come into force. Proceedings begun after that date follow BNSS procedure. The offence is judged under the law in force on the date of the act (Art 20(1)): conduct before 1 July 2024 is an IPC offence, conduct on or after it is a BNS offence, even though the procedure in a fresh FIR is BNSS.

Purpose and philosophy: procedural code - it prescribes machinery for investigation, inquiry, trial and punishment; substantive criminal law lies in the BNS. BNSS adds technology (audio-video recording, electronic summons, e-FIR, electronic trial), time-bound steps, victim-centric provisions and a statutory witness-protection scheme.

Definitions (s.2(1) BNSS; s.2 CrPC): 'cognizable offence' - police may arrest without warrant and investigate without Magistrate's order; 'non-cognizable' - police need a warrant and the Magistrate's order to investigate; 'bailable' and 'non-bailable' as per First Schedule (or other law); 'summons-case' - offence not being a warrant-case; 'warrant-case' - offence punishable with death, imprisonment for life or imprisonment exceeding two years; 'complaint' - allegation made orally, in writing or electronically to a Magistrate with a view to action under the Sanhita (a police report is not a complaint; but a police report that discloses only a non-cognizable offence is treated as a complaint, Explanation); 'police report' - report forwarded under s.193(3) (173(2) CrPC); 'inquiry' - every inquiry other than a trial conducted by a Magistrate or Court; 'investigation' - collection of evidence by police or any person authorised by a Magistrate; 'judicial proceeding' - includes any proceeding in which evidence is or may be legally taken on oath; 'victim' - person who has suffered loss or injury by the act or omission of the accused, including guardian or legal heir; new definitions of 'electronic communication' and 'audio-video electronic means'.

Inquiry v. investigation v. trial: investigation is by police (executive), inquiry by Magistrate/Court before trial (judicial), trial is the determination of guilt (Directorate of Enforcement v. Deepak Mahajan, 1994; Adri Dharan Das v. State of W.B., 2005 - 'arrest' meaning).

Classification of offences: (1) cognizable / non-cognizable; (2) bailable / non-bailable; (3) compoundable / non-compoundable (s.359); (4) summons-case / warrant-case; (5) triable by Court of Session / Magistrate (First Schedule, Part-I for BNS offences, Part-II for other laws: if punishable with death/life/imprisonment above 7 years - Court of Session; otherwise Magistrate).

Trial procedures: Sessions trial (ss.248-260), warrant-case trial by Magistrate on police report (ss.261-266) and on complaint (ss.267-273), summons-case (ss.274-282), summary trial (ss.283-288), plea bargaining (ss.289-300).

Basic principles: presumption of innocence; burden on prosecution; fair trial and open court (s.366 BNSS/327 CrPC; Art 21); speedy trial (Hussainara Khatoon, 1979; A.R. Antulay, 1992 - bar of limitation not applicable to criminal trial but delay violates Art 21); right to be defended (Art 22(1), s.340 BNSS/303 CrPC); free legal aid (s.341 BNSS/304 CrPC; Art 39A; Khatri v. State of Bihar, 1981; Suk Das v. UT of Arunachal Pradesh, 1986 - trial vitiated without legal aid); no double jeopardy (s.337 BNSS/300 CrPC; Art 20(2)); inherent powers (s.528 BNSS/482 CrPC).

Headline BNSS innovations at a glance: zero FIR and e-FIR (s.173); preliminary enquiry for 3-7 year offences (s.173(3)); mandatory forensic visit for 7+ year offences (s.176(3)); audio-video recording of search and seizure (s.105) and of statements; handcuff rule (s.43(3)); arrest safeguard for the infirm/over-60 (s.35(7)); police custody in parts (s.187); proclaimed offender and trial in absentia (ss.84, 356); attachment of proceeds of crime (s.107); victim information within 90 days (s.193(3)(ii)); discharge and charge within 60 days (ss.250-251); documents supplied within 14 days (s.230); judgment within 45 days (s.392); witness protection scheme (s.398); mercy-petition time-lines (s.472); undertrial release rules (s.479); trial in electronic mode (s.530); community service as punishment (BNS s.4(f), s.23 BNSS).

key_provisions.content: Repeal of CrPC and savings: pending proceedings continue under CrPC.
Definitions - includes victim, electronic communication, audio-video electronic means.
Offences under BNS tried per BNSS; offences under other laws tried per BNSS unless the special law provides otherwise.
Savings of special/local law and special jurisdiction; BNSS does not override them.
Classification of BNS offences: cognizable?, bailable?, by which court triable.

sections.title: Constitution and Powers of Criminal Courts; Public Prosecutors; Sentencing Limits
sections.overview: Hierarchy of courts, which court tries what, how much punishment each court may award, and the role of Public Prosecutors and the Directorate of Prosecution.
must_know: Classes of criminal courts (s.6 BNSS; s.6 CrPC): (i) Courts of Session; (ii) Judicial Magistrates of the First Class; (iii) Judicial Magistrates of the Second Class; (iv) Executive Magistrates. The BNSS drops the CrPC's Metropolitan Magistrates and metropolitan areas; the Chief Judicial Magistrate heads the Judicial Magistrates in a district.

Court of Session: established by the State Government for every sessions division; Sessions Judge appointed by the High Court; Additional/Assistant Sessions Judges may be appointed by the High Court. HC may appoint judges of one division to exercise jurisdiction in another.

Subordination: Chief Judicial Magistrate is subordinate to the Sessions Judge; every other Judicial Magistrate is subordinate to the CJM; Additional Sessions Judge exercises powers as directed by the Sessions Judge.

Sentencing powers - High Court and Sessions Judge (s.22 BNSS; s.28 CrPC): High Court - any sentence authorised by law; Sessions Judge/Additional Sessions Judge - any sentence authorised by law but a death sentence must be confirmed by the High Court; Assistant Sessions Judge - imprisonment up to ten years and fine to any amount.

Sentencing powers - Magistrates (s.23 BNSS; s.29 CrPC): CJM - any sentence authorised by law except death, life imprisonment or imprisonment exceeding seven years; Judicial Magistrate First Class - imprisonment up to three years, or fine up to Rs 50,000 (CrPC: Rs 10,000), or both, or community service; Judicial Magistrate Second Class - imprisonment up to one year, or fine up to Rs 10,000 (CrPC: Rs 5,000), or both, or community service.

Default imprisonment on non-payment of fine (s.24 BNSS; s.30 CrPC): not exceeding one-fourth of the maximum term of imprisonment for the offence, and not beyond the Magistrate's power. Consecutive sentences (s.25 BNSS; s.31 CrPC): the aggregate must not exceed twice the maximum the court can impose for a single offence, and must not exceed 14 years (CrPC proviso) in the case of a Magistrate.

Court by which offences triable (s.21 BNSS; s.26 CrPC): offences under BNS - High Court, Court of Session, or any other court shown in First Schedule; offences against other laws - the court mentioned in the law or, failing that, per First Schedule Part II. Offences under certain BNS sections (e.g., ss.64-71 rape-related) are ordinarily tried by a court presided over by a woman judge as far as practicable (s.21 proviso; CrPC 26 proviso).

Executive Magistrates: District Magistrate and Sub-Divisional Magistrate - preventive, security, public-order and maintenance-of-peace functions (ss.125-143, 148-167), not trial of offences generally. Special Executive Magistrates may be appointed.

Public Prosecutors (s.18 BNSS; s.24 CrPC): Central/State Government appoints PP for High Court; for districts, the State Government appoints a PP and Additional PPs from a panel of names prepared by the District Magistrate in consultation with the Sessions Judge; the person must have been an advocate for not less than seven years. Assistant Public Prosecutors (s.19; s.25 CrPC) conduct prosecutions in Magistrate courts; a police officer may be appointed APP only if he has not taken part in the investigation and is not below the rank of Inspector. Director of Prosecution and Deputy/Assistant Directors (s.20; s.25A CrPC) head the Directorate of Prosecution in the State.

Role of the Public Prosecutor: officer of the court and independent (Shiv Kumar v. Hukam Chand, 1999; Thakur Ram v. State of Bihar, 1966). A private lawyer may assist the PP and, with the Magistrate's permission, conduct the prosecution (s.339 BNSS; s.302 CrPC), but the PP remains in charge. The victim may engage an advocate to assist the prosecution (proviso to s.338 BNSS; proviso to s.301(2) CrPC).

Additional safeguards in BNSS on courts: audio-video electronic means may be used for appearances (s.530); courts may sit in any place for convenience if necessary; electronic summons and warrants; the procedure of 'trial in absentia' for proclaimed offenders (s.356).

key_provisions.content: Classes of criminal courts: Session, JMFC, JMSC, Executive Magistrates.
Sentences which High Court and Sessions Judge may pass; ASJ up to 10 years.
Sentences which Magistrates may pass: CJM up to 7 years; JMFC 3 years/Rs 50,000; JMSC 1 year/Rs 10,000.
Public Prosecutors - minimum seven years' standing as advocate.
Directorate of Prosecution.

landmark_cases.case: Rekha Murarka v. State of W.B.

landmark_cases.case: Thakur Ram v. State of Bihar

exam_traps: ASJ's limit is ten years (not seven).
A Sessions Judge may pass a death sentence but cannot execute it until the High Court confirms (s.407 BNSS).
Metropolitan Magistrates no longer exist in BNSS.
PP must have seven years' practice; the policeman-APP condition is different.

sections.title: Arrest of Persons (ss.35-62 BNSS / ss.41-60A CrPC) and Rights of the Arrested Person
sections.overview: One of the most heavily tested clusters. Learn the grounds of arrest without warrant, the notice of appearance, the written grounds rule, 24-hour production, medical examination, handcuffs and the safeguard cases.
must_know: Arrest without warrant by police (s.35(1) BNSS; s.41 CrPC): (a) any person who commits a cognizable offence in the officer's presence; (b) person against whom a reasonable complaint, credible information or reasonable suspicion exists of a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment up to seven years - only if the officer is satisfied that arrest is necessary to prevent further offence, for proper investigation, to prevent evidence disappearing or tampering, to prevent inducement/threat to witnesses, or to ensure presence in court - and he must record reasons in writing; (c) person against whom credible information exists of a cognizable offence punishable with more than seven years or death; (d) proclaimed offender; (e)-(i) possession of stolen property, obstructing a police officer, escapee, deserter, person liable to be extradited, released convict failing to notify address.

Notice of appearance (s.35(3)-(6) BNSS; s.41A CrPC): where arrest is not required under s.35(1), police shall issue a notice directing the person to appear. The person must comply; if he complies, he shall not be arrested unless the officer records reasons for arrest and obtains approval. If he does not comply, he may be arrested (subject to the Court's order).

s.35(7) BNSS (new): for an offence punishable with imprisonment of less than three years, and where the person is infirm or is above sixty years of age, arrest may be made only with the prior permission of an officer not below the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police.

Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2014): arrest is not automatic for offences punishable up to seven years; police must satisfy the conditions of s.41(1)(b) and Magistrates must not authorise detention mechanically. Satender Kumar Antil v. CBI (2022) re-emphasised compliance.

Procedure on arrest (s.36 BNSS; s.41B CrPC): police officer shall bear accurate, visible and clear identification of name; prepare a memorandum of arrest attested by at least one witness who is a family member or a respectable member of the locality, and countersigned by the arrested person; inform the arrested person of the right to have a relative or friend informed. s.37 BNSS (41C CrPC): State to establish control rooms; a designated police officer of rank not below Assistant Sub-Inspector at every police station and district to maintain particulars of arrested persons, and to display them prominently. s.38 BNSS (41D CrPC): arrested person is entitled to meet an advocate of his choice during interrogation, though not throughout (Poolpandi v. Superintendent, Central Excise, 1992; Nandini Satpathy v. P.L. Dani, 1978 - right to silence and counsel's presence).

Arrest by private person (s.40 BNSS; s.43 CrPC): any private person may arrest, or cause to be arrested, a proclaimed offender or a person who in his presence commits a non-bailable and cognizable offence; he must without unnecessary delay hand him over to a police officer or take him to the nearest police station. Arrest by Magistrate (s.41; s.44 CrPC). Protection of members of the Armed Forces (s.42; s.45 CrPC): no arrest for acts done in official duty without the Central Government's consent.

How arrest is made (s.43 BNSS; s.46 CrPC): by actual touch or confinement unless there is submission to custody; if the person forcibly resists, all means necessary may be used; the right to cause death is limited to persons accused of offences punishable with death or life imprisonment; a woman is not to be arrested after sunset or before sunrise except in exceptional circumstances with a written report and prior permission of the Judicial Magistrate of the First Class; for a woman, arrest is by touch only unless circumstances indicate otherwise and, as far as practicable, by a woman police officer. s.43(3) BNSS (new) allows handcuffs, keeping in view the nature and gravity of the offence, for habitual or repeat offenders, persons who escaped from custody, and those accused of organised crime, terrorist act, drug-related crime, illegal possession of arms, murder, rape, acid attack, counterfeiting, human trafficking, sexual offences against children, or offences against the State. Prem Shankar Shukla v. Delhi Administration (1980) and Sunil Batra (1978) restrict handcuffing as a general rule - treated as the baseline.

Search of the arrested person (s.49; s.51 CrPC): search with decency; women only by women; articles taken to be listed and receipt given. s.46 BNSS (s.49 CrPC): no more restraint than necessary to prevent escape.

Right to know grounds and bail (s.47 BNSS; s.50 CrPC): every arrested person must be forthwith informed of the full particulars of the offence and of the grounds of arrest; for bailable offences he must be informed of the right to be released on bail and to arrange sureties. s.48 BNSS (s.50A CrPC): the arrested person's friend, relative or nominee must be informed of the arrest and place; the arresting officer must make a record; the Magistrate must verify compliance.

Mihir Rajesh Shah v. State of Maharashtra (6 Nov 2025; 2025 INSC 1288): under Art 22(1) and s.47 BNSS the grounds of arrest must be furnished in writing, in a language the arrestee understands, in every case under every statute; where oral intimation is necessary at the spot, the written grounds must follow within a reasonable time and in any event at least two hours before production for remand; failure renders the arrest and remand illegal. Earlier: Pankaj Bansal v. Union of India (2023) (PMLA), Prabir Purkayastha v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2024) (UAPA), Vihaan Kumar v. State of Haryana (Feb 2025).

Medical examination: s.51 BNSS (s.53 CrPC) - at the request of police by a registered medical practitioner; s.52 (s.53A) - examination of an accused of rape; s.53 (s.54) - examination at the arrested person's own request, if he alleges torture, to produce evidence; s.54 (s.54A) - identification; s.56 (s.55A) - duty to take reasonable care of the health and safety of the arrested person.

Production before Magistrate: s.57 BNSS (s.56 CrPC) - the arrested person must be taken before a Magistrate or the officer in charge of the police station without unnecessary delay; s.58 (s.57 CrPC) - no detention beyond 24 hours (excluding journey time) without the Magistrate's order; Art 22(2). Release only on bond, bail or the Magistrate's order (s.59; s.58 CrPC).

Custodial safeguards: D.K. Basu v. State of W.B. (1997) - 11 requirements (identification of police, memo, witness, medical check every 48 hours, intimate relative, diary entry, access to lawyer, display at control room); Joginder Kumar v. State of U.P. (1994) - arrest should not be routine; right to inform someone; Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa (1993) and Rudul Sah v. State of Bihar (1983) - compensation for custodial death/illegal detention under Arts 32/226; Sheela Barse v. State of Maharashtra (1983) - women in custody; Inder Mohan Goswami v. State of Uttaranchal (2007) - guidelines for warrants.
Escape and re-arrest (s.60-61 BNSS; ss.59-60 CrPC); s.62 BNSS (s.60A CrPC): no arrest except in accordance with the Sanhita or any other law.

Related constitutional safeguards: Art 22(1) (grounds and counsel), Art 22(2) (24 hours), Art 22(3)-(7) (preventive detention not covered by 22(1)-(2)), Art 20(3) (self-incrimination), Art 21 (procedure fair, just, reasonable).

key_provisions.content: Arrest without warrant by police: cognizable offence, reasonable suspicion, reasons to be recorded.
Notice of appearance in lieu of arrest.
New safeguard: persons over 60 or infirm, offences under 3 years - DSP permission.
Grounds of arrest - now to be in writing per Mihir Rajesh Shah (2025).
24-hour limit on detention without Magistrate's order.
Handcuffs - for specified categories of offenders.

Art 22(1)-(2) do not apply to preventive detention or enemy aliens.
Right to meet advocate is during interrogation, not throughout.
probable_questions: Which section of BNSS corresponds to s.41 CrPC? (s.35)
What is the time limit for producing an arrested person before a Magistrate? (24 hours)
A woman may not be arrested between sunset and sunrise except with whose permission? (JMFC)
Under BNSS, for an infirm person above 60, arrest for an offence below 3 years requires permission of? (DSP)

sections.title: Process to Compel Appearance: Summons, Warrants, Proclamation and Attachment
sections.overview: Difference between summons and warrant, bailable and non-bailable warrants, service on corporate bodies, electronic summons, proclamation for absconders, attachment and the BNSS 'proclaimed offender' reforms.
must_know: Summons (ss.63-71 BNSS; ss.61-69 CrPC): in writing, in duplicate, signed by the presiding officer or by such officer as the High Court may direct, bearing the court's seal; specifies time and place; served by a police officer or an officer of the court or public servant; served personally by delivering/tendering a copy (BNSS adds service by electronic communication: s.64(2) - the summons bears the image of the court's seal and is served by electronic means as per rules). Service on corporate bodies (secretary, local manager, director or by registered post to the principal officer); service when the person cannot be found (leave with an adult family member; if none, affix to the house); service on a Government servant through the head of his office; service outside local jurisdiction.

Summons v. warrant: summons is an order to appear; warrant is an order to arrest and produce. Summons is the general mode in a summons-case; in a warrant-case the Magistrate may issue either (s.227 BNSS; s.204 CrPC). Court may issue a warrant in lieu of or in addition to summons if the person fails to appear or the court believes he will not (s.89 BNSS; s.87 CrPC).

Warrants of arrest (s.72 onwards BNSS; ss.70-81 CrPC): in writing, signed by presiding officer, bearing seal; remains in force until cancelled or executed (s.72); court may direct by endorsement that a person be released if he gives bail with surety - a 'bailable warrant' (s.73; s.71 CrPC); directed to police officers or, if urgent, to any other person (s.75; s.73 CrPC); the officer must notify the substance of the warrant and, on request, show it; a person arrested must be brought without delay before the court; warrants may be executed outside the jurisdiction with the help of the local Magistrate/police.

Non-bailable warrants should be issued only for good reason - Inder Mohan Goswami v. State of Uttaranchal (2007): consider seriousness, possibility of absconding, previous history, whether summons were served; Court must first try summons, then bailable warrant, then non-bailable warrant, then proclamation.

Proclamation for person absconding (s.84 BNSS; s.82 CrPC): if the court has reason to believe that a person against whom a warrant has been issued has absconded or is concealing himself, it may publish a written proclamation requiring him to appear within not less than thirty days. The proclamation is read publicly in the town/village, affixed to the house and to the court-house, and also published in a daily newspaper. BNSS s.84 also lets the court declare a person a 'proclaimed offender' in respect of grave offences (those punishable with imprisonment of ten years or more, life or death) if he fails to appear.

Attachment of property of absconder (s.85 BNSS; s.83 CrPC): after proclamation the court may attach movable or immovable property of the person; claims and objections (s.86; s.84 CrPC) within six months; release, sale and restoration (s.87; s.85 CrPC). The BNSS adds a provision for identification, attachment and forfeiture of property of a proclaimed person, including property abroad through letters of request (s.86 - [VERIFY section letter]).
Bonds for appearance (s.90 BNSS; s.88 CrPC): any court may require a person present before it to execute a bond with or without sureties to appear. s.91 (s.89): arrest on breach of the bond.
Provisions applicable to summons and warrants (s.92 BNSS; s.90 CrPC): the chapter's provisions apply to every summons and warrant issued under the Sanhita.

Lavesh v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2012): 'absconding' under s.82 CrPC means deliberate hiding. Court must satisfy itself on the facts before proclamation; a person declared proclaimed offender cannot ordinarily get anticipatory bail (Lavesh; Prem Shankar Prasad v. State of Bihar, 2021 - noted in 2026 digests).

key_provisions.content: Summons may be served by electronic communication bearing the image of the court's seal.
Form of warrant of arrest - in force until cancelled or executed.
Proclamation for absconding person - 30 days to appear.
Attachment of property of absconder.
Warrant in lieu of or in addition to summons.

landmark_cases.case: Inder Mohan Goswami v. State of Uttaranchal
landmark_cases.held: Guidelines for issuing non-bailable warrants; liberty to be balanced; reasons required.

landmark_cases.case: Lavesh v. State (NCT of Delhi)
landmark_cases.held: Absconder who has been proclaimed an offender cannot normally claim anticipatory bail.

landmark_cases.case: Pepsi Foods v. Special Judicial Magistrate
landmark_cases.held: Summoning order requires application of mind.

landmark_cases.case: State of Punjab v. Sarwan Singh
landmark_cases.held: Limitation not a bar to summons in certain circumstances; proclaiming process.

landmark_cases.case: Raghubans Dubey v. State of Bihar
landmark_cases.held: Cognizance is of the offence; once taken, the Magistrate may proceed against all those involved.

mnemonics: Escalation of process: Summons -> Bailable warrant -> Non-bailable warrant -> Proclamation (30 days) -> Attachment -> Proclaimed offender -> Trial in absentia (s.356).
exam_traps: Proclamation applies to persons (accused) who abscond; not to witnesses.
30 days is the minimum period given in the proclamation.
Proclaimed offender status under BNSS is limited to serious offences.
probable_questions: How many days must a proclamation give the absconder to appear? (Not less than 30)
Which BNSS section corresponds to s.82 CrPC? (s.84)
Can summons be served electronically under BNSS? (Yes - s.64(2))

sections.title: Process to Compel Production of Things; Search and Seizure; Reciprocal Arrangements with Foreign Countries
sections.overview: Summons to produce, search warrants, how a search must be conducted (including the new mandatory audio-video recording), seizure by police, attachment of proceeds of crime, and cross-border cooperation.
must_know: Summons to produce document or other thing (s.94 BNSS; s.91 CrPC): a court, or a police officer in charge of a police station, may summon any person in whose possession a document or thing is believed to be, if necessary or desirable for investigation or trial. BNSS clarifies that 'document or other thing' includes electronic communication and digital devices - so that digital evidence can be summoned. Exception: documents in postal/telegraph custody (s.95; s.92 CrPC). Compliance by producing the thing, not necessarily by attending.

Search warrants (s.96 BNSS; s.93 CrPC): issued where (a) the court has reason to believe a person summoned under s.94 will not produce the document; (b) it is not known who possesses it; or (c) the court considers that a general search or inspection will serve the purposes. The warrant may be directed to specified places; the Magistrate may specify the part of the house.

Search of place suspected to contain stolen property, forged documents (s.97; s.94 CrPC) by a District or Sub-divisional Magistrate; power to declare certain publications forfeited (s.98; s.95 CrPC) - State Government; application to the High Court to set aside forfeiture (s.99; s.96 CrPC) within two months; search for persons wrongfully confined (s.100; s.97 CrPC); power to compel restoration of abducted persons (s.101; s.98 CrPC).

Conduct of a search (ss.102-103 BNSS; ss.99-100 CrPC): the person in charge of a closed place must allow free ingress; the officer may break open doors if refused after demand; search to be made in the presence of two or more independent and respectable inhabitants of the locality (or, if none are available, from another locality); a list of things seized is prepared and signed by the witnesses; a copy given to the occupant; a woman's person is searched only by a woman with strict regard to decency; the occupier is entitled to be present. BNSS s.105 (new): the process of search and seizure, including preparation of the list of seized articles and the signing by witnesses, shall be recorded through audio-video electronic means, preferably by mobile phone, and the recording forwarded forthwith to the District Magistrate/Sub-divisional Magistrate/Chief Judicial Magistrate.

Disposal of things found in search beyond jurisdiction (s.104; s.101 CrPC). Police seizure (s.106 BNSS; s.102 CrPC): any police officer may seize any property alleged or suspected to have been stolen, or found under circumstances which create suspicion of an offence, and must report it forthwith to the Magistrate. The Supreme Court has held that bank accounts can be seized/frozen under s.102 CrPC (Tapas Neogy v. State of W.B., 1999; Teesta Setalvad v. State of Gujarat, 2018) - the provision cannot be used for immovable property (Nevada Properties v. State of Maharashtra, 2019).

Attachment, forfeiture or restoration of property (s.107 BNSS; new): where the police officer investigating has reason to believe that any property is proceeds of crime, he may, with the Magistrate's approval, apply for attachment; the Magistrate may attach it after hearing; if the offence results in conviction the Court may order distribution to those affected; if the accused is acquitted/discharged the property is restored. 'Proceeds of crime' is defined as property derived or obtained directly or indirectly from criminal activity, including its value.

Police search without warrant (s.185 BNSS; s.165 CrPC): an officer in charge of a police station or investigating officer may search or cause search where he has reasonable grounds to believe that thing necessary for investigation cannot otherwise be obtained without undue delay; he must record the grounds in writing; search must be recorded by audio-video means; a copy is sent to the nearest Magistrate. s.186 (s.166): an officer may require another officer to search.

Evidentiary effect of illegal search: illegality in search does not by itself make seized evidence inadmissible; the court examines whether there was prejudice or violation of a safeguard (Pooran Mal v. Director of Inspection, 1974; Radhakishan v. State of U.P., 1963; R.M. Malkani v. State of Maharashtra, 1973). Compare Art 20(3) and s.349 BNSS (s.311A CrPC): a Magistrate may order any person to give specimen signatures or handwriting; Ritesh Sinha v. State of U.P. (2019): voice samples may be ordered; Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010): narco-analysis, polygraph, brain-mapping without consent are impermissible.

Reciprocal arrangements for assistance in certain matters (Chapter VIII BNSS; Chapter VIIA CrPC, ss.105A-105L): letters of request to courts or authorities in countries with reciprocal arrangements for investigation or evidence; attachment and forfeiture of property in India or abroad derived from crime committed in a contracting State; BNSS expands these provisions and ties them to proceeds of crime and extradition [VERIFY section-level numbering of ss.111-124]. Letters rogatory (earlier CrPC ss.166A-166B) are now dealt with in the BNSS chapter on investigation/ reciprocal arrangements.

key_provisions.content: Summons to produce document or thing - now covers electronic devices.
Mandatory audio-video recording of search and seizure.
Police power to seize property suspected stolen or found in suspicious circumstances.
Attachment, forfeiture or restoration of property which is proceeds of crime.
Search by police without warrant - reasons recorded; A/V recording.

landmark_cases.held: Illegally obtained evidence is admissible unless excluded by statute or Constitution.

landmark_cases.case: State of Punjab v. Baldev Singh
landmark_cases.held: Search of person under NDPS - option of Magistrate/gazetted officer; non-compliance vitiates recovery.

landmark_cases.case: Tapas Neogy v. State of W.B.
landmark_cases.held: Bank account is 'property' for s.102 CrPC; police can seize.

landmark_cases.case: Teesta Setalvad v. State of Gujarat
landmark_cases.held: Seizure/freezing under s.102 must be reported to Magistrate forthwith.

landmark_cases.case: Nevada Properties Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra
landmark_cases.held: s.102 does not cover immovable property.

landmark_cases.case: Ritesh Sinha v. State of U.P.

landmark_cases.case: Selvi v. State of Karnataka
landmark_cases.held: Involuntary narco/polygraph/BEAP tests violate Art 20(3) and Art 21.

mnemonics: Search checklist: 'W-L-C-R' - Witnesses (2 independent), List, Copy to occupant, Recording (audio-video, new).
exam_traps: s.94 is the successor to s.91 and covers digital devices; s.105 is new.
s.106 (police seizure) cannot be used for immovable property; s.107 (attachment of proceeds of crime) is the route.
Illegal search does not automatically exclude evidence (Indian position), unlike US.

Which BNSS section provides for attachment of proceeds of crime? (s.107)
How many independent witnesses are required for a search? (Two)

sections.title: Security Proceedings, Maintenance of Wives, Children and Parents, Public Order and Preventive Action by Police
sections.articles: BNSS ss.125-172 (CrPC ss.106-153); maintenance ss.144-147 (CrPC ss.125-128); s.163 (CrPC s.144)
sections.overview: Maintenance (s.144 BNSS = s.125 CrPC) and s.163 (old s.144) are AIBE favourites. Also know security for peace/good behaviour, dispersal of unlawful assemblies, public nuisance and police preventive arrests.
must_know: Security for keeping the peace and good behaviour (Executive Magistrates): s.125 BNSS (s.106 CrPC) - on conviction; s.126 (s.107) - security for keeping the peace in other cases (likely breach of peace); s.127 (s.108) - security for good behaviour from persons disseminating certain matters (those promoting disaffection, class hatred or defamatory threats); s.128 (s.109) - security for good behaviour from vagrants and suspected persons; s.129 (s.110) - security from habitual offenders (up to three years). Bonds with or without sureties, for periods up to one year (peace) or three years (habitual offenders). Cases: Madhu Limaye v. State of Maharashtra (1970) - preventive jurisdiction valid.

Maintenance of wives, children and parents (s.144 BNSS; s.125 CrPC): a person having sufficient means who neglects or refuses to maintain (a) his wife (including a divorced wife who has not remarried), unable to maintain herself; (b) his legitimate or illegitimate minor child (married or not); (c) his major child (not a married daughter) who is physically or mentally disabled and unable to maintain himself; or (d) his father or mother unable to maintain himself/herself - may be ordered by a Magistrate of the First Class to pay a monthly allowance (no ceiling since 2001), payable from the date of order or, if so ordered, from the date of application. Interim maintenance and expenses of proceedings may be ordered; the application for interim maintenance is to be disposed of within 60 days from service of notice (proviso).

Disqualifications of the wife (s.144(4) BNSS; s.125(4)): she is living in adultery, refuses without sufficient reason to live with her husband, or they are living separately by mutual consent. Wife is entitled to maintenance even if she is living separately for a justifiable reason such as cruelty or second marriage (Chaturbhuj v. Sita Bai, 2008).

Procedure: proceedings may be taken in any district where the person resides, where the wife resides or where he last resided with the wife; evidence recorded in the presence of the person against whom the order is proposed (or his advocate); alteration/cancellation on change of circumstances (s.146; s.127 CrPC); enforcement through warrants to levy the amount as fines and imprisonment up to one month (s.147; s.128 CrPC). The remedy is secular and applies to persons of all religions (Shah Bano, 1985; Danial Latifi v. Union of India, 2001; Shabana Bano v. Imran Khan, 2009; Mohd. Abdul Samad v. State of Telangana, 2024 - a divorced Muslim woman can apply under s.125 CrPC / s.144 BNSS, with the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act 1986 as an additional remedy).

Rajnesh v. Neha (2021): guidelines to harmonise maintenance proceedings - mandatory affidavit of disclosure of assets, income and liabilities; maintenance from the date of application; set-off; execution; overlapping jurisdiction (Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act, DV Act, CrPC/BNSS). Bhuwan Mohan Singh v. Meena (2014): speedy disposal; Badshah v. Urmila Badshah Godse (2014): purposive interpretation including de facto wives. Capt. Ramesh Chander Kaushal v. Veena Kaushal (1978): parents' maintenance is a social obligation. [Cross-ref Part 6 Family Law.]

Unlawful assemblies (s.148 BNSS; s.129 CrPC): dispersal by an Executive Magistrate or officer in charge of a police station by civil force/command; use of armed forces (s.149; s.130) - Magistrate of highest rank; duty of officers (s.150; s.131); protection against prosecution for acts done in good faith under these sections (s.151; s.132) - sanction needed.

Public nuisances (s.152 BNSS; s.133 CrPC): conditional order to remove nuisance by DM/SDM/Executive Magistrate; if not obeyed, the person may show cause or the order becomes absolute; Vasant Manga Nikumba v. Baburao Bhikanna (1995): nuisance cannot be removed with delay.

Orders in urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger (s.163 BNSS; s.144 CrPC): the District Magistrate, Sub-divisional Magistrate or any Executive Magistrate empowered by the State Government may issue a written order directing a person to abstain from a certain act or to take certain order with respect to property where there is sufficient ground for proceeding and immediate prevention or speedy remedy is desirable; may be ex parte; the order remains in force for two months (extendable by the State Government up to six months, and if necessary to prevent danger to human life, health or safety, or a riot or affray); the Magistrate may rescind or alter on application; the order must be reasoned. Cases: Babulal Parate v. State of Maharashtra (1961) - s.144 valid; Madhu Limaye (1970) - power of Executive Magistrate subject to judicial review; Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) - orders must be published, proportionate, reasoned and for a limited period; Ramlila Maidan Incident, In re (2012) - right to assemble and right to sleep; Amit Sahni v. Commissioner of Police (2020) - public roads cannot be occupied indefinitely.

Disputes as to immovable property likely to cause a breach of the peace (s.164 BNSS; s.145 CrPC): Executive Magistrate may declare possession; (s.165; s.146) attachment pending decision; (s.166; s.147) disputes regarding right of use of land or water.

Preventive action by police (ss.168-172 BNSS; ss.149-153 CrPC): police may intervene to prevent commission of cognizable offences (s.168); information of design to commit a cognizable offence (s.169); arrest to prevent commission of cognizable offences (s.170; s.151 CrPC) - the person must not be detained beyond 24 hours unless required by any other provision; prevention of injury to public property (s.171; s.152); inspection of weights and measures (s.172; s.153).

key_provisions.content: Maintenance of wife, children, parents; interim maintenance within 60 days.
Alteration in allowance.
Orders in urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger; 2 months, extendable to 6.
Security for keeping the peace in other cases.
Arrest to prevent commission of cognizable offences.

landmark_cases.held: s.125 CrPC applies to Muslim divorced wives; secular remedy.

landmark_cases.case: Danial Latifi v. Union of India
landmark_cases.held: Upheld the 1986 Act but read it to provide a fair provision for the divorced wife beyond iddat.

landmark_cases.case: Mohd. Abdul Samad v. State of Telangana
landmark_cases.held: Divorced Muslim women can seek maintenance under s.125 CrPC; the 1986 Act does not oust it.

landmark_cases.case: Rajnesh v. Neha
landmark_cases.held: Guidelines on disclosure affidavit, interim maintenance, date of maintenance.

landmark_cases.case: Babulal Parate v. State of Maharashtra
landmark_cases.held: s.144 valid as reasonable restriction under Art 19.

landmark_cases.case: Madhu Limaye v. SDM, Monghyr
landmark_cases.held: s.144 is not an arbitrary power; Magistrate must act judicially.

landmark_cases.case: Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India
landmark_cases.held: s.144 orders subject to proportionality, publication and review.

landmark_cases.case: Chaturbhuj v. Sita Bai
landmark_cases.held: Wife living separately for sufficient reason can claim maintenance; provision is a measure of social justice.

mnemonics: Maintenance beneficiaries: 'W-C-C-P' - Wife, minor Child, disabled adult Child, Parents.
s.163 = 2 months / 6 months.
exam_traps: Maintenance cannot be ordered for a married daughter (even a minor married daughter qualifies only through the husband); minor married child is covered only if she herself is unable.
Divorced wife is covered until she remarries.
s.163 BNSS is NOT s.144 CrPC maintenance; maintenance is s.144 BNSS (old s.125). Do not mix the numbers.
probable_questions: Which BNSS section deals with maintenance of wife, children and parents? (s.144)
Order under s.163 BNSS remains in force for? (2 months, extendable to 6)
Is there a maximum limit on maintenance? (No)

sections.title: Information to Police, FIR, Investigation, Remand, Default Bail and Police Report
sections.overview: The single most important block. Zero FIR, e-FIR, preliminary enquiry, power to investigate, Magistrate's order for investigation (s.175(3)/(4)), examination of witnesses, confessions, remand (s.187), default bail and the final report (s.193).
must_know: FIR (s.173(1) BNSS; s.154 CrPC): information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence, given orally or by electronic communication to the officer in charge of a police station, irrespective of the area where the offence was committed ('Zero FIR'); if oral, it is reduced to writing, read over and signed; if by electronic communication, it must be signed within three days to be taken on record; recorded in the prescribed book; informant gets a copy free of cost (s.173(2)). Rape and sexual offences (BNS ss.64-71): information recorded by a woman police officer; if the victim is temporarily or permanently mentally or physically disabled, it is recorded at the victim's residence or a convenient place, in the presence of an interpreter or special educator, with videography.

Preliminary enquiry (s.173(3) BNSS; new): for offences punishable with three years or more but less than seven years, the officer in charge may, with the prior permission of an officer not below the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police, conduct a preliminary enquiry within fourteen days to ascertain whether a prima facie case exists, or proceed with investigation. For offences punishable with seven years or more, an FIR must be registered.

Lalita Kumari v. Government of U.P. (2014, Constitution Bench): registration of an FIR is mandatory if the information discloses a cognizable offence; no preliminary inquiry in such cases; preliminary inquiry is permitted only to find whether a cognizable offence is disclosed and only in categories such as matrimonial/family disputes, commercial offences, medical negligence, corruption cases, and cases with abnormal delay (more than three months without satisfactory explanation); inquiry to be concluded within a week (now 14 days under BNSS for the 3-7 years category). Failure to register: erring officer is liable to action (BNS s.199 (IPC s.166A)). Zero FIR: Satvinder Kaur v. State (Govt of NCT of Delhi), 1999 - jurisdiction is no ground for refusing registration, but investigation must be by the competent police station.

Refusal to register FIR (s.173(4) BNSS; s.154(3) CrPC): the aggrieved person may send the substance of the information in writing or by post (or electronically) to the Superintendent of Police, who must either investigate or direct investigation; if SP does not act, the informant may apply to the Magistrate under s.175(3) BNSS (s.156(3) CrPC); remedy under Art 226 also available. Delay in lodging FIR: explainable delay is not fatal (State of H.P. v. Gian Chand, 2001); FIR is not substantive evidence; used to corroborate/contradict the maker (Hasib v. State of Bihar, 1972). Second FIR for the same incident is barred (T.T. Antony v. State of Kerala, 2001) but a counter-version FIR is permitted (Upkar Singh v. Ved Prakash, 2004); 'test of sameness' - Amish Devgan v. Union of India (2020).

Information as to non-cognizable cases (s.174 BNSS; s.155 CrPC): enter in the book and refer the informant to the Magistrate; no investigation without the Magistrate's order; if a case involves both, it is treated as cognizable.

Police power to investigate (s.175 BNSS; s.156 CrPC): an officer in charge may investigate any cognizable case which a court having jurisdiction would have power to try; no proceeding of a police officer is invalid on the ground that he lacked power. s.175(3): any Magistrate empowered under s.210 may order investigation, after considering the application supported by an affidavit under s.173(4), after making such inquiry as he thinks necessary and after considering the submission of the police officer (new). s.175(4) (new): where the complaint is against a public servant arising in the course of official duty, the Magistrate may order investigation only after receiving a report containing facts and circumstances from the superior officer and after considering the assertions of the public servant about the situation that led to the incident. The Supreme Court (Jan 2026 and Oct 2026) held that s.175(4) is a procedural adjunct to s.175(3), not a standalone provision, and that it expands safeguards for public servants beyond the old s.156(3) [VERIFY].

Magistrate's s.156(3)/175(3) power: Sakiri Vasu v. State of U.P. (2008) - Magistrate can direct registration and monitor investigation; Priyanka Srivastava v. State of U.P. (2015) - affidavit and prior approach to police/SP are mandatory; Anil Kumar v. M.K. Aiyappa (2013) - sanction under s.197 CrPC is required before the Magistrate orders investigation against a public servant; an April 2026 Supreme Court ruling reportedly held that no prior sanction is needed merely to direct FIR registration under s.156(3)/s.175(3) [VERIFY]; State of Bihar v. J.A.C. Saldanha (1980) - courts should not interfere with the statutory investigation; Vinubhai Haribhai Malaviya v. State of Gujarat (2019) - Magistrate can order further investigation up to the stage trial begins/ concludes.

Procedure for investigation (s.176 BNSS; s.157 CrPC): where there is reason to suspect a cognizable offence, the officer proceeds in person to the spot, investigates facts, and takes measures to discover and arrest the offender; may depute a subordinate for trivial matters. s.176(3) BNSS (new): for offences punishable with imprisonment of seven years or more, a forensic expert shall visit the crime scene to collect forensic evidence and the process shall be videographed on a mobile phone or other electronic device; if a State lacks forensic facility, it shall notify a facility in another State.

Power to require attendance of witnesses (s.179 BNSS; s.160 CrPC): a police officer making an investigation may, by written order, require any person acquainted with the facts to attend; a male person under the age of 15 years or above 60 years (CrPC: 65), a woman, or a mentally or physically disabled person shall not be required to attend any place other than the place of residence. Examination of witnesses by police (s.180; s.161 CrPC): oral examination; the person is bound to answer truly all questions except those which tend to expose him to a criminal charge, penalty or forfeiture; statements may be recorded by audio-video means; statements of women victims of offences under BNS ss.64-71 etc. to be recorded by a woman police officer.

Statements to police (s.181 BNSS; s.162 CrPC): not to be signed; not to be used for any purpose at any inquiry or trial except to contradict the witness (Tahsildar Singh v. State of U.P., 1959) - exceptions: dying declarations, statements leading to discovery (BSA s.23(2)), and statements in FIR.

Recording of confessions and statements (s.183 BNSS; s.164 CrPC): a Judicial Magistrate (not a police officer) may record a confession or statement made during investigation, whether or not the Magistrate has jurisdiction; the Magistrate must explain that the person is not bound to make a confession and that it may be used as evidence; he must be satisfied that it is voluntary; no police officer to be present; confessions can be recorded by audio-video means; the person must be given time for reflection if he is produced from police custody; a statement of a person alleging offences under BNS ss.64-71 etc. must be recorded by a Judicial Magistrate, if possible a woman, as soon as the commission of the offence is brought to notice; a disabled victim's statement is to be recorded with an interpreter or special educator and videographed, which then has the value of examination-in-chief and need not be repeated at trial.

Medical examination of rape victim (s.184 BNSS; s.164A CrPC): by a registered medical practitioner employed in a Government hospital (or any registered medical practitioner with the consent of the woman/guardian), within twenty-four hours of receiving information; report forwarded to the investigating officer within seven days, who forwards it to the Magistrate.

Search by police officer (s.185-186). Remand and detention (s.187 BNSS; s.167 CrPC): when investigation cannot be completed within 24 hours (Art 22(2)), the officer forwards the accused to the nearest Magistrate with a copy of the case-diary entries; the Magistrate (even without jurisdiction) may authorise detention for a term not exceeding fifteen days in the whole (police custody or otherwise); beyond fifteen days, only judicial custody; maximum detention: ninety days where the investigation relates to an offence punishable with death, life imprisonment or imprisonment of ten years or more; sixty days for any other offence; on the expiry of that period the accused shall be released on bail if he is prepared to and does furnish bail ('default bail', 'statutory bail', 'indefeasible right'). BNSS allows police custody to be taken in whole or in parts within the first forty days (for 60-day offences) or the first sixty days (for 90-day offences) [VERIFY the exact formulation and judicial treatment]. An Executive Magistrate may authorise detention for seven days at a time where no Judicial Magistrate is available. The accused must be produced physically or via audio-video means.

Default bail jurisprudence: Chaganti Satyanarayana v. State of A.P. (1986) - Art 21; Central Bureau of Investigation v. Anupam J. Kulkarni (1992) - police custody only within first fifteen days; Sanjay Dutt v. State (1994) - indefeasible right; Uday Mohanlal Acharya v. State of Maharashtra (2001) - right must be exercised before the chargesheet is filed; Rakesh Kumar Paul v. State of Assam (2017) - 'not less than ten years' means a minimum of ten years; so the 90-day limit applies only to offences with minimum 10 years or death/life, and 60 days to others; Bikramjit Singh v. State of Punjab (2020) - UAPA extension must be by a Court; M. Ravindran v. Intelligence Officer, DRI (2021) - the right accrues on expiry, even if application is made later; filing of an incomplete chargesheet to defeat default bail is impermissible; Ritu Chhabaria v. Union of India (2023) - investigation not complete merely because the chargesheet is filed incompletely.

Release of accused when evidence deficient (s.189 BNSS; s.169 CrPC) and cases sent to Magistrate when evidence is sufficient (s.190; s.170); diary of proceedings in investigation (s.192; s.172 CrPC) - to be maintained day-to-day; courts may use it to aid in inquiry or trial but not as evidence; accused has no right to call for it (Mukund Lal v. Union of India, 1989; Khatri v. State of Bihar, 1981 - subject to s.172(3) and s.145 Evidence Act).

Police report (s.193 BNSS; s.173 CrPC): on completion of investigation, a report is forwarded to the Magistrate (by electronic means also); investigation of rape (BNS ss.64-71 etc.) to be completed within two months from the date of recording the information (s.193(2)); contents (s.193(3)): names of parties, nature of information, names of persons acquainted with the circumstances, whether any offence appears to have been committed and by whom, whether the accused has been arrested, released on bond or bail, forwarded in custody, and whether the medical examination report of the woman is attached; s.193(3)(ii) (new): the police must inform the victim or informant, within ninety days, of the progress of the investigation by any means including electronic communication; the Magistrate has to take cognizance or may direct further investigation. s.193(9) (new in text, per Vinubhai principle): further investigation after the report is permitted, with the court's permission if the trial has commenced, and should be completed within ninety days (extendable with permission).

Closure report: the Magistrate may accept, reject (and take cognizance or issue process), or direct further investigation; the informant must be given notice and an opportunity to file a protest petition (Bhagwant Singh v. Commissioner of Police, 1985); the Magistrate cannot compel the police to file a charge-sheet but can take cognizance on the material (Abhinandan Jha v. Dinesh Mishra, 1967).

Inquests: s.194 BNSS (s.174 CrPC): police inquest on unnatural deaths - report to the nearest Magistrate; s.196 (s.176 CrPC): Magistrate's inquiry into the cause of death in police custody, disappearance, or rape in custody is mandatory; Magistrate may hold inquest in other cases (exhumation allowed).

Quashing of FIR: State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal (1992) - seven categories; R.P. Kapur v. State of Punjab (1960); Neeharika Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra (2021) - courts to exercise the power sparingly and not to stay investigations in routine manner.

Investigation - miscellany: Custodial interrogation permitted but torture banned (Art 21); statements under pressure are inadmissible (BSA s.22-23); investigation officer's duty to maintain case diary; special investigative agencies (CBI/ NIA) may need State consent under DSPE Act s.6 (State of W.B. v. Committee for Protection of Democratic Rights, 2010 - Art 226 can order CBI inquiry in exceptional cases).

sections.title: Jurisdiction, Cognizance, Complaints to Magistrates, Sanction and Commitment of Cases
sections.overview: Place of inquiry and trial, conditions for cognizance, how a complaint is processed (including the new accused-hearing proviso), sanction, bar on cognizance, supply of documents and commitment to the Court of Session.
must_know: Ordinary place of inquiry and trial (s.197 BNSS; s.177 CrPC): the court within whose local jurisdiction the offence was committed; offences committed in one of several local areas, or continuing offences, may be tried in any (ss.198-199); the offence may be tried where the act was done or where the consequence ensued (s.199; s.179 CrPC); trial at place where the victim was found; offences by travel on journeys; offences committed outside India (s.208; s.188 CrPC) require the Central Government's sanction.

Conditions for initiating proceedings (Chapter XIV BNSS): cognizance of offences by Magistrates (s.210 BNSS; s.190 CrPC): a Magistrate of the first class (or second class if specially empowered) may take cognizance of an offence (a) upon receiving a complaint of facts which constitute such offence (including by electronic means); (b) upon a police report of such facts; (c) upon information received from any person other than a police officer, or upon his own knowledge. Cognizance is taken of the offence and not of the offender (Raghubans Dubey v. State of Bihar, 1967; Pastor P. Raju v. State of Bihar). 'Taking cognizance' means application of judicial mind to the facts with a view to proceeding (R.R. Chari v. State of U.P., 1951; Subramanian Sethuraman v. State of Maharashtra, 2004).

Transfer on application of the accused (s.211; s.191 CrPC), making over to Magistrates (s.212), cognizance by Courts of Session (s.213 BNSS; s.193 CrPC): the Court of Session cannot take cognizance as a court of original jurisdiction unless the case has been committed to it by a Magistrate; Dharam Pal v. State of Haryana (2014, Constitution Bench): after committal, the Sessions Court may under s.193 CrPC (s.213 BNSS) summon additional persons against whom a prima facie case appears.

Bar on cognizance: (i) s.215 BNSS (s.195 CrPC): offences against public servants' lawful authority (contempt-type offences under the BNS chapter on contempts of lawful authority of public servants), offences against public justice (false evidence etc.) and offences relating to documents given in evidence - only on a written complaint by the public servant concerned or by the court concerned; Sachida Nand Singh v. State of Bihar (1998); Iqbal Singh Marwah v. Meenakshi Marwah (2005) - forged documents produced in court: the bar applies only if the forgery occurred after the document was in custodia legis; (ii) s.217 BNSS (s.196 CrPC): offences against the State (including BNS s.152 successor of sedition-type offences) and criminal conspiracy to commit them - only on the Central or State Government's complaint/sanction; (iii) s.218 (s.197 CrPC): prosecution of Judges, Magistrates and public servants for acts in the course of official duty requires previous sanction of the appropriate government - BNSS (new) requires the government to decide within 120 days of receiving the request, failing which sanction is deemed granted [VERIFY]; Matajog Dobey v. H.C. Bhari (1956) - 'reasonable connection' test; D. Devaraja v. Owais Sabeer Hussain (2020) - 'colour of duty'; Subramanian Swamy v. Manmohan Singh (2012) - three months for decision plus one month for legal consultation; Vineet Narain v. Union of India (1998); BNS/BNSS and PC Act s.19/17A cross-ref; (iv) s.222 (s.199 CrPC): prosecution for defamation - only on a complaint by the person aggrieved (with special rules for President, Governors, Ministers and public servants, which may be by the Public Prosecutor with sanction); offences relating to marriage (s.219-221 BNSS) - only on complaint by the aggrieved spouse/relative.

Complaints to Magistrates (Chapter XV BNSS; Chapter XV CrPC): examination of complainant (s.223 BNSS; s.200 CrPC): the Magistrate taking cognizance of an offence on complaint shall examine upon oath the complainant and witnesses present and reduce the substance of the examination to writing, signed by the complainant, witnesses and the Magistrate; no examination is necessary when the complaint is in writing made by a public servant in the discharge of official duties or by a court. The BNSS (new proviso) provides that no cognizance of an offence shall be taken by the Magistrate without giving the accused an opportunity of being heard. [Cross-ref courts: the proviso is read to apply to complaint cases, not to police reports.]

Postponement of issue of process (s.225 BNSS; s.202 CrPC): the Magistrate may postpone issue of process and either inquire himself or direct an investigation by a police officer or other person; it is mandatory to do so where the accused resides beyond the area of the Magistrate's jurisdiction. If the offence is triable exclusively by the Court of Session, the Magistrate shall call upon the complainant to produce all witnesses. Dismissal of the complaint (s.226; s.203): if there is no sufficient ground for proceeding, the reasons are recorded in brief. Issue of process (s.227; s.204): if in the opinion of the Magistrate there is sufficient ground for proceeding, a summons (summons-case) or warrant or summons (warrant-case) is issued; no process is issued until the list of witnesses is filed and fees paid. Dispensing with personal attendance (s.228; s.205).

Principles on summoning: Pepsi Foods (1998) - summoning is serious; Kewal Krishan v. Suraj Bhan (1980) - at s.203 stage only prima facie and not detailed merits; Mehmood Ul Rehman v. Khazir Mohammad Tunda (2015) - inquiry must be reasoned; Birla Corporation Ltd v. Adventz Investments (2019) - inquiry or investigation is mandatory for accused beyond jurisdiction; GHCL Employees Stock Option Trust v. India Infoline Ltd (2013); Jagdish Ram v. State of Rajasthan (2004).

Commencement of proceedings (ss.227-228): s.227 issue of process; s.228 dispensing with personal attendance; s.229 (s.206) special summons in cases of petty offences (by post, fine up to Rs 1,000); s.230 BNSS (s.207 CrPC): supply of police report and documents (FIR, police report, statements recorded, confessions, other documents) to the accused free of cost without delay and in any case within fourteen days from the date of production or appearance (new time-limit; earlier 'forthwith'); documents may be furnished electronically; voluminous documents may be supplied in electronic form. s.231 (s.208): supply of copies in cases triable by Court of Session instituted otherwise than on police report. s.232 (s.209): commitment - when it appears that the offence is triable exclusively by the Court of Session, the Magistrate commits the case after complying with s.230 or s.231; notifies the PP; sends record and exhibits. s.233 (s.210): where a complaint case and a police investigation relate to the same offence, the Magistrate stays the complaint proceedings and calls for the police report; if the police report names persons who are also accused in the complaint, both are tried together as if instituted on a police report; otherwise the complaint proceeds independently.

Cognizance in 'complaint v. police report': An accused may be summoned only if the Magistrate is satisfied that material exists. Chargesheet may be accepted though the investigating officer opined no case; the Magistrate has independent discretion (Abhinandan Jha, 1967; Bhagwant Singh, 1985). For offences exclusively triable by sessions, the Magistrate has only the committal function; he cannot discharge the accused at that stage.

Limitation for taking cognizance: s.514 BNSS (s.468 CrPC): six months for offence punishable with fine only; one year for imprisonment up to one year; three years for imprisonment exceeding one year but not exceeding three years; no limit for offences punishable with more than three years; s.515 (s.469) commencement; s.516 (s.470) exclusion of time; s.518 (s.472) continuing offences; s.519 (s.473) court may condone delay in the interest of justice. Sarah Mathew v. Institute of Cardio Vascular Diseases (2014, Constitution Bench): the relevant date is the date of filing the complaint or initiating criminal proceedings, not the date of cognizance. The period is computed per the punishment prescribed for the gravest offence.

sections.title: The Charge: Form, Contents, Alteration, Joinder and Discharge
sections.overview: What a charge must contain, when it may be altered, separate and joint trial rules, and the standard for discharge/framing of charge (now with 60-day limits).
must_know: Charge (s.234-237 BNSS; ss.211-214 CrPC): every charge states the offence with which the accused is charged; the law and section; the specific name of the offence if it has one, otherwise the definition; particulars as to time, place, person against whom, or thing in respect of which, the offence was committed (s.235; s.212); in cases of criminal breach of trust or dishonest misappropriation, it is enough to specify gross sum and dates between which the offence was committed (s.235 - as in s.212(2) CrPC) - and the total period must not exceed one year. The manner of commission may be specified where needed (s.236; s.213). The charge is written in the language of the court; read and explained to the accused.

Effect of errors (s.238 BNSS; s.215 CrPC; s.510-511 BNSS (ss.464-465 CrPC)): an error or omission in the charge is not material unless the accused was in fact misled and it occasioned a failure of justice. Willie (William) Slaney v. State of M.P. (1955): the test is prejudice; the court looks at whether the accused knew what he was being tried for. Absence of charge is a curable irregularity unless prejudice (s.510).

Alteration of charge (s.239 BNSS; s.216 CrPC): any court may alter or add to a charge at any time before judgment is pronounced; every alteration is read and explained; if the alteration is not likely to prejudice the accused, the trial proceeds; otherwise the court may direct a new trial or adjourn; sanction is required if the new charge needs sanction. s.240 (s.217): recall of witnesses on alteration. Court cannot convict for an offence for which the charge was not framed unless it is a minor offence (s.245 BNSS; s.222 CrPC) or cognate offence with no prejudice. Dr. Nallapareddy Sridhar Reddy v. State of A.P. (2020); Kantilal Chandulal Mehta v. State of Maharashtra (1969).

Separate charges for distinct offences (s.241; s.218 CrPC): for every distinct offence a separate charge and trial; exceptions: three offences of the same kind within twelve months (s.242; s.219 CrPC); offences committed in the course of the same transaction (s.243; s.220 - one trial); doubt as to which of several offences has been committed - charge in the alternative (s.244; s.221); where the accused is charged with an offence and facts proved reduce it to a minor offence, he may be convicted of the minor (s.245; s.222). Persons who may be charged jointly (s.246; s.223 CrPC): persons accused of the same offence or offences committed in the course of the same transaction, or abetment/attempt, or offences of the same kind committed in conjunction. Withdrawal of remaining charges (s.247; s.224).

Framing of charge/discharge in a Sessions case (s.250-251 BNSS; ss.227-228 CrPC): after committal and hearing both sides, if the Judge considers that there is no sufficient ground for proceeding, he discharges the accused after recording reasons (s.250); the application for discharge is to be made by the accused within sixty days from the date of commitment (new time-limit). If there is ground for presuming that the accused has committed an offence triable by a Magistrate, he may frame a charge and transfer the case to the CJM; if triable exclusively by the Court of Session, he frames a charge in writing (s.251); the charge shall be framed within sixty days from the date of the first hearing on charge (new time-limit); the charge is read and explained and the accused is asked whether he pleads guilty or claims to be tried.

Standard for charge: only a prima facie case; the Judge may sift and weigh the material to the extent of finding if a prima facie case exists, but cannot conduct a mini-trial (Union of India v. Prafulla Kumar Samal, 1979; Sajjan Kumar v. CBI, 2010; Amit Kapoor v. Ramesh Chander, 2012; State of Rajasthan v. Ashok Kumar Kashyap, 2021). Strong suspicion is enough to frame a charge; grave suspicion not rebutted - Onkar Nath Mishra v. State (NCT of Delhi), 2008. The accused has no right to produce defence material at the charge stage (State of Orissa v. Debendra Nath Padhi, 2005 - Constitution Bench - though the Court in Nitya Dharmananda v. Gopal Sheelum Reddy, 2018 allowed sterling-quality documents in rare cases).

Discharge in warrant cases on police report (s.262 BNSS; s.239 CrPC) and on complaint (s.268; s.245): Magistrate discharges where the charge is groundless, recording reasons; if not discharged, charge is framed (s.263; s.240 CrPC).
Joint trial of accused: s.246 BNSS; separate trials may be ordered where joinder causes prejudice. Misjoinder is an irregularity curable under s.511 BNSS unless prejudice is shown.
Charge as the foundation: trial without a charge in Sessions and warrant cases is irregular; in summons-cases the 'substance of the accusation' is stated (s.274; s.251 CrPC).

sections.title: Trial before a Court of Session
sections.overview: Stage-by-stage sessions trial: PP, opening, discharge, charge, plea, evidence, s.351 examination, acquittal, defence, arguments, judgment, hearing on sentence.
must_know: Sequence of a sessions trial: committal (s.232) -> PP conducts prosecution (s.248; s.225) -> opening of the case by the prosecution describing the charge and the evidence (s.249; s.226) -> hearing on discharge (s.250; s.227) -> framing of charge (s.251; s.228) -> plea of guilty or claim to be tried (s.252; s.229) -> date for prosecution evidence and summoning of witnesses (s.253; s.230) -> prosecution evidence (s.254; s.231) -> examination of the accused (s.351 BNSS; s.313 CrPC) -> acquittal if no evidence (s.255; s.232) -> defence entered (s.256; s.233) -> arguments (s.257; s.234) -> judgment of acquittal or conviction, and if convicted, hearing on sentence (s.258; s.235) -> previous conviction (s.259; s.236).

Plea of guilty (s.252; s.229): the Judge may convict on the plea in his discretion; the plea must be voluntary and unambiguous; courts are cautious in capital cases (the Judge should not convict on a plea in a case involving death sentence without recording evidence).

Evidence for prosecution (s.254; s.231): the Judge takes all such evidence as is produced; may permit cross-examination to be deferred; evidence may be recorded in audio-video mode (s.530). s.255 (s.232): after taking evidence and examining the accused, if the Judge considers that there is no evidence that the accused committed the offence, he shall record an order of acquittal.

Entering upon defence (s.256; s.233): the accused is called upon to enter upon his defence and adduce evidence; the accused may file a written statement; the Judge issues process for compelling attendance of defence witnesses unless he considers the application vexatious or for delay.

Arguments (s.257; s.234): the prosecution sums up its case and the defence replies; if the accused adduces evidence, the prosecution may reply; point of law may be argued with permission; oral arguments are heard and written submissions may be filed. BNSS requires judgment to be delivered within forty-five days of the completion of arguments (s.392(1)), with the copy uploaded within seven days.

Judgment and sentence (s.258; s.235): after the arguments the Judge gives a judgment of acquittal or conviction; if convicted, the Judge shall hear the accused on the question of sentence (unless he proceeds under s.401 probation) and pass sentence (Santa Singh v. State of Punjab, 1976 - hearing on sentence is mandatory; Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab, 1980 - death sentence in the 'rarest of rare' case, special reasons; Manoj v. State of M.P., 2022 - the court must call for mitigating material and a psychological/prison report before awarding death).
Procedure in cases instituted under s.199(2) CrPC (defamation of high functionaries) - s.260 BNSS (s.237 CrPC).

Sessions trial: PP leads prosecution; evidence of the accused as a competent witness only on his request (s.353; s.315); witnesses protection (s.398 BNSS); court may call material witnesses (s.348; s.311 CrPC); evidence may be taken on commission (s.319-325; ss.284-290).

Principles of appreciating evidence: five golden principles of circumstantial evidence (Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra, 1984 - Hanumant Govind Nargundkar, 1952); conviction on the sole testimony of an injured witness; interested witnesses - Masalti v. State of U.P. (1965); hostile witness - Bhagwan Singh v. State of Haryana (1976); Zahira Habibullah Sheikh v. State of Gujarat (2004, 2006) - fair trial and the role of the court as an active participant; PW not to be turned away by delay; test identification parade; dying declaration - Laxman v. State of Maharashtra (2002). [Cross-ref Part 5 Evidence.]

sections.title: Trial of Warrant-cases, Summons-cases, Summary Trials and Plea Bargaining
sections.overview: The Magistrate's trial procedures. Know who may try which category, the procedure steps, summary trial limits and the eligibility conditions for plea bargaining.
must_know: Warrant-cases on police report (ss.261-266 BNSS; ss.238-243 CrPC): compliance with s.230 (supply of documents); discharge if the charge is groundless (s.262); framing of charge (s.263) - in writing and read to the accused; plea of guilty (s.264); evidence for prosecution (s.265) - the Magistrate hears the prosecution and takes all evidence; evidence for defence (s.266). Warrant-cases on complaint (ss.267-273 BNSS; ss.244-250 CrPC): evidence for prosecution (s.267); discharge (s.268; s.245); procedure where accused not discharged (s.269); evidence for defence (s.270); acquittal or conviction (s.271; s.248); absence of complainant (s.272; s.249) - the Magistrate may discharge the accused if offence is compoundable or non-cognizable; compensation for accusation without reasonable cause (s.273; s.250) - the Magistrate may order the complainant or informant to pay compensation to the accused.

Summons-cases (ss.274-282 BNSS; ss.251-259 CrPC): substance of the accusation is stated to the accused (no formal charge) (s.274); conviction on plea of guilty (s.275); conviction on plea of guilty in absence of accused in petty cases (s.276; s.253 - fine not exceeding Rs 1,000 sent by post/through pleader); procedure (s.277); acquittal or conviction (s.278); non-appearance or death of the complainant (s.279; s.256) - the Magistrate may acquit the accused unless he adjourns; withdrawal of complaint (s.280; s.257) - with Magistrate's permission; power to stop proceedings in certain cases (s.281; s.258) - the Magistrate of the first class with the CJM's previous sanction may stop proceedings in a summons-case instituted otherwise than on a complaint and release/acquit; power to convert summons-cases into warrant-cases (s.282; s.259) - where the offence is punishable with imprisonment exceeding six months and the Magistrate thinks it in the interests of justice.

Summary trials (ss.283-288 BNSS; ss.260-265 CrPC): the Chief Judicial Magistrate, a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class specially empowered by the High Court, may try summarily offences not punishable with death, imprisonment for life or imprisonment exceeding three years (CrPC: two years) - along with theft, receiving stolen property, assisting concealment, etc. where the value does not exceed Rs 20,000 [VERIFY value limit]; No appeal in petty cases; no sentence of imprisonment exceeding three months in a summary trial (s.285; s.262 CrPC). The procedure is that of a summons-case; a record of the date, offence, plea, evidence, finding and sentence is kept (s.286; s.263); a judgment is brief (s.287; s.264). BNSS also provides that a Magistrate shall try summarily certain petty cases (those punishable with fine only up to a small limit [VERIFY]) and promotes community service as a sentence for petty offences.

Plea bargaining (Chapter XXIII BNSS ss.289-300; Chapter XXIA CrPC ss.265A-265L): applies to offences other than those punishable with death, imprisonment for life or imprisonment exceeding seven years; excluded: offences affecting the socio-economic condition of the country, and offences committed against a woman or a child below fourteen years of age (BNSS s.289; s.265A). The accused must file an application in the court of trial within thirty days from the date of framing of charge (s.289(1)), accompanied by an affidavit stating that he has voluntarily preferred it and has not been previously convicted of the same offence. The court examines the accused in camera to satisfy that the application is voluntary; issues notice to the PP/complainant/victim; a mutually satisfactory disposition is worked out; the victim is entitled to compensation; the sentence may be less than the minimum (half of the minimum where a minimum is provided; one-fourth of the punishment otherwise) and the accused may be released on probation (s.265E CrPC; corresponding BNSS section in the s.289-300 block). The judgment is final and no appeal lies except an SLP under Art 136 or writ under Arts 226/227 (s.265G CrPC; corresponding BNSS section in the s.289-300 block). The statements made by the accused in plea-bargaining cannot be used for any other purpose (s.265K). Set-off of detention period applies (s.468). Plea bargaining is not available to juveniles (separate regime).

Plea bargaining cases: State of Gujarat v. Natwar Harchandji Thakor (2005) - Gujarat HC upheld the constitutionality in the context of the new chapter; Murlidhar Meghraj Loya v. State of Maharashtra (1976) and Kasambhai v. State of Gujarat (1980) - plea bargaining in socio-economic offences was disapproved.
Attendance of persons confined or detained in prisons (Chapter XXII BNSS) - production before court by video-conferencing is permitted under BNSS.

Judgment in summary trials: the Magistrate records: serial number of the case, date of commission, date of complaint, the offender's name, parentage and residence, the offence and value of property, plea and examination, finding, sentence, date of termination.
