sections.title: General Provisions on Inquiries and Trials: Evidence, Examination of Accused, Pardon, Adjournment, Additional Accused, Compounding, Withdrawal, Absentia Trial, Unsound Mind
sections.articles: BNSS ss.301-391 (CrPC ss.266-352): ss.308-336 (evidence), 337-366 (general), 367-378 (unsound mind), 379-391 (offences affecting administration of justice)
sections.overview: A high-scoring cluster: s.337 double jeopardy, s.343 approver, s.346 adjournment, s.348 summoning witnesses, s.351 accused's examination, s.356 trial in absentia, s.358 additional accused, s.359 compounding, s.360 withdrawal.
must_know: Evidence in the presence of the accused (s.308 BNSS; s.273 CrPC): all evidence is taken in the presence of the accused or his advocate; evidence by audio-video electronic means is allowed; examination of the witness by video-conferencing is valid (State of Maharashtra v. Dr. Praful B. Desai, 2003). Recording of evidence in summons-, warrant- and sessions cases (ss.309-311; ss.274-276 CrPC): by the Magistrate/Judge in narrative form; language of record; memorandum when the Magistrate cannot record; demeanour remarks (s.315; s.280). Evidence of medical witnesses (s.326; s.291 CrPC); reports of Government scientific experts (s.328; s.293 CrPC) - the Director of Forensic Science Laboratory and others - may be used as evidence without calling the expert, though the court may summon him; no formal proof of certain documents (s.329; s.294 CrPC); evidence on affidavit of a formal character (s.331; s.296 CrPC); evidence of public servants, experts and police officers by electronic means (s.336 - new [VERIFY]).

Double jeopardy (s.337 BNSS; s.300 CrPC): a person who has been tried by a competent court for an offence and convicted or acquitted shall not be tried again for the same offence, or for any other offence on the same facts for which a different charge might have been made under s.242(1) (s.221) or for which he might have been convicted under s.243(2) (s.222). Exceptions: acquittal/discharge withdrawn; different offence with consequence not known at the time; offences resulting in a different consequence; the Court was not competent. Art 20(2); State of Bombay v. S.L. Apte (1961); Kolla Veera Raghav Rao v. Gorantla Venkateswara Rao (2011).

Legal aid to accused at State expense (s.341 BNSS; s.304 CrPC): where the accused has no pleader and the court considers him unable to engage one, the court shall assign a pleader at State expense in a trial before the Court of Session (and High Court may extend to other courts); Khatri v. State of Bihar (1981); Suk Das v. Union Territory of Arunachal Pradesh (1986) - failure to provide legal aid vitiates the trial. Right to be defended by a pleader (s.340; s.303 CrPC).

Tender of pardon to an accomplice (s.343 BNSS; s.306 CrPC): a CJM at any stage of investigation or inquiry, and a Magistrate of the First Class at the inquiry or trial, may tender pardon on the condition of making a full and true disclosure of the whole of the circumstances within his knowledge relating to the offence and to every other person concerned; applies to offences triable exclusively by the Court of Session or by the Special Judge, offences punishable with imprisonment of seven years or more; s.344 (s.307): after commitment, the Court of Session may tender pardon; s.345 (s.308): trial of a person who fails to comply with the condition of pardon; Suresh Chandra Bahri v. State of Bihar (1994); Bangaru Laxman v. State (2012) - Court's duty on pardon; the approver is a competent witness (Evidence Act/BSA) but his evidence needs corroboration in material particulars.

Power to postpone or adjourn proceedings (s.346 BNSS; s.309 CrPC): proceedings are to be continued from day to day until all the witnesses in attendance have been examined; adjournments only for special reasons recorded in writing; no adjournment merely to enable a party to show cause against sentence; costs may be imposed; once the evidence has begun, the case should proceed day to day and not be adjourned beyond the next day (Vinod Kumar v. State of Punjab, 2015 - day-to-day trial; Hussain v. Union of India, 2017 - time-bound trials). Where witnesses are present, no adjournment without examining them unless there are special reasons recorded in writing. The remand of accused in custody may not exceed fifteen days at a time.

Local inspection (s.347; s.310); power to summon material witness or examine person present (s.348 BNSS; s.311 CrPC): at any stage of an inquiry, trial or other proceeding, the Court may summon any person as a witness, or examine any person in attendance, or recall and re-examine any person already examined, if his evidence appears essential to the just decision of the case; it is the duty of the court to do so, and the court is not confined by the prosecution's list (Zahira Habibullah Sheikh, 2006; Mohanlal Shamji Soni v. Union of India, 1991; Rajendra Prasad v. Narcotic Cell, 1999). s.349 BNSS (s.311A CrPC): Magistrate may order any person (including an arrested person) to give specimen signature or handwriting.

Power to examine the accused (s.351 BNSS; s.313 CrPC): the Court may at any stage and shall, after the prosecution witnesses have been examined and before the accused is called for his defence, question him generally on the case to enable him to explain any circumstances appearing in the evidence against him; he is not on oath; the court cannot draw adverse inference from refusal to answer; the answers may be taken into consideration in the inquiry or trial and may be put in evidence for or against him in any other inquiry or trial for any other offence which such answers may tend to show he committed. The court must put every material incriminating circumstance to the accused; omission may vitiate the conviction if prejudice is shown (Asraf Ali v. State of Assam, 2008; Reena Hazarika v. State of Assam, 2019; Premchand v. State of Maharashtra, 2023). The accused may now give his statement through audio-video electronic means in specified situations. s.352 (s.314) oral arguments and memoranda; s.353 (s.315): accused is a competent defence witness on his own request, no adverse comment on his not giving evidence; s.354 (s.316): no influence by promise or threat; s.355 (s.317): dispensing with personal attendance of the accused during inquiries and trials where he is represented by pleader.

Trial and judgment in absentia of proclaimed offender (s.356 BNSS; new): where a person declared a proclaimed offender has absconded to evade trial and there is no immediate prospect of arresting him, the trial may proceed in his absence as if he were present and judgment may be pronounced. Conditions (as reported): framing of charge; at least ninety days after the framing of charge; two successive notices by publication in a national or local daily at an interval of thirty days; service on the relative or last-known address; recording of reasons; appointment of a State-paid advocate to represent him; the person is allowed to appear at any stage subject to the court's conditions; no appeal against conviction unless he appears within three years of the judgment [VERIFY details] . Absence trial has been compared with s.299 CrPC (record of evidence in absence of accused).

Procedure where accused does not understand proceedings (s.357; s.318 CrPC); power to proceed against other persons appearing to be guilty (s.358 BNSS; s.319 CrPC): where, in the course of an inquiry or trial, it appears from the evidence that any person not being the accused has committed an offence for which he could be tried together with the accused, the court may proceed against him and he is added; the court may detain him and the proceedings are commenced afresh; the trial of such person starts afresh. Hardeep Singh v. State of Punjab (2014, Constitution Bench): the power can be exercised on the basis of evidence adduced at trial (even examination-in-chief); the standard is higher than prima facie but lower than that for conviction - 'strong and cogent evidence'; to be exercised sparingly; applies after the commencement of the trial; also to the Sessions Court, even in absence of committal of that person; Brijendra Singh v. State of Rajasthan (2017); Sarabjit Singh v. State of Punjab (2009); Labhuji Amratji Thakor v. State of Gujarat (2019).

Compounding of offences (s.359 BNSS; s.320 CrPC): Table 1 - offences compoundable by the persons mentioned without the court's permission (e.g., hurt, wrongful restraint, defamation, adultery-type offences as re-enacted, criminal trespass, mischief of certain kinds); Table 2 - offences compoundable with the court's permission (e.g., voluntarily causing hurt by dangerous weapons, theft, cheating, criminal breach of trust of a limited kind). The composition has the effect of an acquittal. Non-compoundable offences cannot be compounded but may be quashed under s.528 on settlement (Gian Singh v. State of Punjab, 2012; Narinder Singh v. State of Punjab, 2014; Parbatbhai Aahir v. State of Gujarat, 2017; Ram Gopal v. State of M.P., 2021 - heinous and serious offences excluded). Offence under s.138 NI Act is compoundable (s.147 NI Act; Damodar S. Prabhu v. Sayed Babalal H., 2010). [Cross-ref Part 7 (NI Act), Part 9 (ADR).]

Withdrawal from prosecution (s.360 BNSS; s.321 CrPC): the Public Prosecutor or Assistant PP in charge of a case may, with the consent of the court, at any time before judgment is pronounced, withdraw from the prosecution of any person; under BNSS the court shall not permit withdrawal without hearing the victim (new). Sheonandan Paswan v. State of Bihar (1987) - consent is a judicial function; Abdul Karim v. State of Karnataka (2000); State of Kerala v. K. Ajith (2021) - withdrawal for political reasons rejected; Bar of withdrawal in cases pending against MPs/MLAs without High Court's permission (Ashwini Upadhyay v. Union of India, 2021 - HC permission required).

Procedure for accused of unsound mind (ss.367-378 BNSS; ss.328-339 CrPC): where the Magistrate/Court has reason to believe that the accused is of unsound mind and incapable of making his defence, he shall inquire into the fact of such unsoundness and cause examination by a psychiatrist or clinical psychologist; trial is postponed; the accused may be released on bail with surety or kept in safe custody in a mental health establishment; resumed when he is fit. If the accused is found to be of unsound mind at the time of the act, the defence of insanity applies (BNS s.22 (IPC s.84)). Mental Healthcare Act 2017 applies.

Offences affecting the administration of justice (ss.379-391 BNSS; ss.340-352 CrPC): procedure for offences under BNS ss.206-229 relating to false evidence, contempt, forged documents given in evidence; the Court may make a complaint after preliminary inquiry; appeals from orders under s.379 are provided; summary procedure for contempt in the presence of the court (s.345 CrPC; corresponding BNSS section in the s.379-391 block).

Open court and in camera trial (s.366 BNSS; s.327 CrPC): the place in which any Criminal Court is held for inquiring into or trying any offence shall be an open court to which the public may have access; for BNS ss.64-71 (rape) trials, in camera trial is mandatory; no publication of the proceedings without the court's permission (BNS s.72 (IPC s.228A) - victim's identity). Nipun Saxena v. Union of India (2019) - identity of victims of sexual offences.

sections.title: Judgment, Sentencing, Compensation to Victims, Probation, Witness Protection and Confirmation of Death Sentence
sections.overview: Contents and timing of judgments, victim compensation, new witness protection scheme, probation, no alteration after signing, and High Court confirmation of death sentences.
must_know: Judgment (s.392 BNSS; s.353 CrPC): pronounced in open court by the presiding officer either immediately after the termination of the trial or at some subsequent time of which notice is given; BNSS requires pronouncement within forty-five days from the date of completion of arguments (reasons to be recorded for any delay in the court record), and the judgment must be made available to the parties electronically within seven days [VERIFY numbers]. Language and contents (s.393; s.354): in the language of the court; points for determination, the decision and reasons; in a conviction, the offence and section of law; in an acquittal, the offence of which the accused is acquitted and a direction that he be set at liberty; where the conviction is for an offence punishable with death or life imprisonment, the judgment should state the reasons for the sentence awarded - for death, 'special reasons' (s.393(3); s.354(3)).

Order for notifying address of previously convicted offender (s.394; s.356 CrPC). Order to pay compensation (s.395 BNSS; s.357 CrPC): when a court imposes a fine, it may order the whole or part to be applied in payment of expenses, compensation to any person for loss or injury, compensation to dependants (fatal accidents), or to the bona fide purchaser of stolen property; when the sentence does not include a fine, the court may order the accused to pay compensation to the victim (s.357(3)); Hari Singh v. Sukhbir Singh (1988) - courts should liberally use compensation; Ankush Shivaji Gaikwad v. State of Maharashtra (2013) - the court has a duty to consider compensation in every case.

Victim compensation scheme (s.396 BNSS; s.357A CrPC): every State Government, in coordination with the Central Government, shall prepare a scheme for compensation to the victim or his dependants who have suffered loss or injury as a result of the crime and who require rehabilitation; the court may recommend compensation; the District/State Legal Services Authority decides the quantum; interim treatment s.397 (s.357C): all hospitals - public or private - shall provide first-aid or medical treatment free of cost to victims of acid attack, rape, and certain sexual offences (BNS ss.64-71 etc.) and shall immediately inform the police. Nipun Saxena v. Union of India (2019); Laxmi v. Union of India (2014) - acid attack victims, compensation of Rs 3 lakh minimum, regulation of acid sales; Delhi Domestic Working Women's Forum v. Union of India (1995) - rape victim compensation; Bodhisattwa Gautam v. Subhra Chakraborty (1996).

Witness protection scheme (s.398 BNSS; new): every State Government shall prepare and notify a Witness Protection Scheme for the State with a view to ensuring the protection of witnesses. Mahender Chawla v. Union of India (2018) - the Supreme Court approved the Witness Protection Scheme, 2018 as law under Art 141 until legislation; Zahira Habibullah (2004); Sakshi v. Union of India (2004) - safeguards for child witnesses.

Compensation to persons groundlessly arrested (s.399; s.358 CrPC) - Magistrate may order compensation up to Rs 1,000 [VERIFY] to the person arrested; costs on frivolous complaints (s.400; s.359). Order to release on probation of good conduct or after admonition (s.401 BNSS; s.360 CrPC): in cases of persons not under twenty-one years convicted of an offence punishable with a fine only or with imprisonment for seven years or less; women convicted of offence not punishable with death or life; and persons under twenty-one convicted of offence not punishable with death or life; the court must consider the age, character, antecedents, circumstances; s.402 (s.361): special reasons to be recorded if probation is not applied. The Probation of Offenders Act 1958 takes precedence; Ved Prakash v. State of Haryana (1981); Rattan Lal v. State of Punjab (1964) - the beneficial provision applies even to pre-Act offences; Chhanni v. State of U.P. (2006); Lakhvir Singh v. State of Punjab (2021). Also see Juvenile Justice Act 2015 (cross-ref Part 10).

No alteration of judgment once signed (s.403 BNSS; s.362 CrPC): save to correct a clerical or arithmetical error (functus officio); Hari Singh Mann v. Harbhajan Singh Bajwa (2001); State of Punjab v. Davinder Pal Singh Bhullar (2011) - inherent powers cannot recall a judgment on merits. Copy of judgment to the accused free of cost (s.404; s.363); judgment in translation (s.405; s.364); copy to be sent to the District Magistrate (s.406; s.365).

Confirmation of death sentence (ss.407-412 BNSS; ss.366-371 CrPC): when the Court of Session passes a sentence of death, the proceedings are submitted to the High Court and the sentence is not executed unless confirmed (s.407; s.366); the HC may direct further inquiry or additional evidence (s.408; s.367); confirm, annul, alter or order a new trial (s.409; s.368); confirmation by at least two Judges (s.410; s.369); procedure if there is a difference of opinion (s.411; s.370: third Judge); order of confirmation (s.412; s.371). The convict has an independent right of appeal to the High Court; the HC must independently scrutinise the evidence. Mohd. Arif @ Ashfaq v. Registrar, Supreme Court (2014): review in death sentence cases is heard in open court by three Judges; Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India (2014) - delay in execution; Santosh Kumar Satishbhushan Bariyar v. State of Maharashtra (2009); Swamy Shraddananda (2008) - life imprisonment for the remainder of life; Union of India v. V. Sriharan (2016, Constitution Bench) - fixed-term life imprisonment without remission up to a specified number of years by the High Court/Supreme Court is permissible; death sentence executed by hanging (Deena v. Union of India, 1983 - constitutional).

sections.title: Appeals, Reference, Revision and Transfer of Criminal Cases
sections.overview: Who may appeal and to which court, victim's right to appeal, appeals against acquittal, powers of appellate court, suspension of sentence, revision and its bars, and transfer powers.
must_know: No appeal unless expressly provided (s.413 BNSS; s.372 CrPC). Proviso: the victim has the right to prefer an appeal against any order passed by the Court acquitting the accused or convicting for a lesser offence or imposing inadequate compensation, and such appeal lies to the court to which an appeal ordinarily lies against the conviction. Satya Pal Singh v. State of M.P. (2015) and Mallikarjun Kodagali v. State of Karnataka (2018): the victim need not seek leave and may appeal even against acquittal.

Appeal from orders requiring security or refusing to accept or rejecting sureties (s.414; s.373 CrPC). Appeals from convictions (s.415 BNSS; s.374 CrPC): (1) from a conviction by a High Court in its extraordinary original criminal jurisdiction - to the Supreme Court; (2) from a conviction by a Sessions Judge or an Additional Sessions Judge, or in a trial in which a sentence of imprisonment for more than seven years has been passed against him or any other person convicted at the same trial - to the High Court; (3) from any other conviction by a Magistrate - to the Court of Session. No appeal where the accused has pleaded guilty and been convicted on his plea, except as to the extent or legality of the sentence (s.416; s.375 CrPC). Petty cases (s.417; s.376): no appeal in the cases of small punishment [VERIFY the thresholds]. Appeal by the State Government against the sentence for enhancement (s.418; s.377).

Appeal against acquittal (s.419 BNSS; s.378 CrPC): the District Magistrate may, in any case instituted on a police report, direct the Public Prosecutor to present an appeal to the Court of Session against an order of acquittal passed by a Magistrate in respect of a cognizable and non-bailable offence; the State Government may direct the Public Prosecutor to appeal to the High Court from an order of acquittal passed by any court (other than a High Court) or an order of acquittal passed by the Court of Session in revision; in cases instituted otherwise than on a police report (complaint cases), the High Court's special leave is required; the complainant may apply for special leave to appeal against acquittal in a complaint-case (to the High Court); the application must be made within sixty days (six months if the complainant is a public servant) [VERIFY]; under BNSS, no appeal on behalf of the State shall be entertained without the leave of the High Court, and the application for leave by the State requires an opportunity to the accused to be heard. Chandrappa v. State of Karnataka (2007) - principles for appeals against acquittal (double presumption of innocence; interference only if view is perverse or impossible); Babu v. State of Kerala (2010).

Powers of the appellate court (ss.427-428 BNSS; ss.386-387 CrPC): may dismiss the appeal, in an appeal from conviction reverse the finding and sentence and acquit or discharge or order re-trial, alter the finding, or reduce the sentence; it may not enhance the sentence in an appeal by the accused alone (an appeal by the State/revision is required, with notice). Summary dismissal (s.425; s.384). Appellate court may take further evidence (s.432; s.391). Judgments of the appellate court (s.429-430). Suspension of sentence pending appeal; release on bail (s.430 BNSS; s.389 CrPC): the appellate court may, for reasons recorded, order that the execution of the sentence or order be suspended and, if he is in confinement, that he be released on bail or on his own bond; for sentences of death or imprisonment for life, or of ten years or more, the PP's opportunity to oppose is mandatory; Bhagwan Rama Shinde Gosavi v. State of Gujarat (1999) and Kishori Lal v. Rupa (2004) - the principles; Atul Tripathi v. State of U.P. (2014); Saudan Singh v. State of U.P. (2021) - a liberal approach; Angana v. State of Rajasthan (2009); Anil Kumar Yadav v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2018) - convicts with sentence 5+ years.

Abatement of appeals (s.435; s.394): an appeal against conviction abates on the death of the appellant (other than an appeal against a sentence of fine); the appeal by the accused may continue by relatives in certain cases. Reference to the High Court (s.436 BNSS; s.395 CrPC): a court may refer to the High Court a question as to the validity of an Act, ordinance or regulation, where the determination is necessary for disposal of a case pending before it and it is of the opinion that the Act is invalid and has not been so declared. The High Court decides the question and the court disposes accordingly.

Revision (ss.438-443 BNSS; ss.397-402 CrPC): the High Court or any Sessions Judge may call for and examine the record of any proceeding before any inferior criminal court within its jurisdiction to satisfy itself as to the correctness, legality or propriety of any finding, sentence or order, and as to the regularity of any proceedings (s.438; s.397). No revision in relation to any interlocutory order (s.438(2); s.397(2)): Amar Nath v. State of Haryana (1977), Madhu Limaye v. State of Maharashtra (1977) - 'interlocutory' is limited to orders of a purely interim or temporary nature and not matters which affect or decide the rights of parties; V.C. Shukla v. State (Delhi Admn.) (1980); K.K. Patel v. State of Gujarat (2000); Girish Kumar Suneja v. CBI (2017) - interlocutory v. intermediate orders. Where an application has been made to either the High Court or Sessions Judge, no further application by the same person is to be entertained by the other (s.438(3); s.397(3)).

Powers of High Court in revision (s.442 BNSS; s.401 CrPC): may exercise any of the powers of an appellate court; may order an inquiry; no order to the prejudice of the accused shall be made unless he has had an opportunity of being heard; no conversion of a finding of acquittal into one of conviction (s.442(3); s.401(3)); no revision where an appeal lies and no appeal has been brought (s.442(4); s.401(4)) - the High Court may treat the revision as an appeal if the party would have been entitled to appeal. Sessions Judge's powers (s.440-441; s.399-400). Power to withdraw/transfer cases within Session division (s.443; s.402). Revision is not a substitute for appeal; revisional power is to be exercised sparingly and for 'perversity', 'palpable error' or 'jurisdictional error' (Pathumma v. Muhammad, 1986; State of Kerala v. Puttumana Illath Jathavedan Namboodiri, 1999; Amit Kapoor v. Ramesh Chander, 2012).

Transfer of criminal cases (ss.447-451 BNSS; ss.406-410 CrPC): the Supreme Court (s.447; s.406) - on application of the Attorney General/ a party, may transfer a case or appeal from one High Court to another, or from a Criminal Court subordinate to one HC to a court subordinate to another HC, whenever it is made to appear that such an order is expedient for the ends of justice; the application is to be supported by affidavit and frivolous applications may attract compensation to the other side; Maneka Sanjay Gandhi v. Rani Jethmalani (1979) - transfer where a reasonable apprehension of unfair trial; Zahira Habibullah Sheikh (2004); Nahar Singh Yadav v. Union of India (2011). The High Court (s.448; s.407) may transfer within its jurisdiction; the Sessions Judge (s.449; s.408) may transfer within the division.

Extra: Appeal to Supreme Court (Art 134, Art 136, Criminal Appeal jurisdiction) and Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act 1970 - where HC reverses acquittal and sentences to death/life/10 years, appeal lies as of right.

sections.title: Execution, Suspension, Remission and Commutation of Sentences; Mercy Petitions
sections.overview: How sentences are executed, set-off of pre-trial detention, remission, commutation, the 14-year rule for life convicts and the new mercy-petition time-lines.
must_know: Execution of death sentence: after confirmation, a warrant is issued; hanging until dead; postponement in the case of a pending appeal/SLP; pregnant woman - the HC may commute to life imprisonment (BNSS provisions replacing ss.413-416 CrPC) [VERIFY section numbers]. Execution of sentences of imprisonment (warrant to the jail); levy of fine (warrant for attachment and sale of movable property; Collector); fine and imprisonment in default.

Set-off of period of detention (s.468 BNSS; s.428 CrPC): the period of detention undergone by the accused during investigation, inquiry or trial is set off against the term of imprisonment imposed on conviction; for a life sentence it is not set off (Bhagirath v. Delhi Administration, 1985 - life imprisonment is for life; State of Maharashtra v. Najakat Alia Mubarak Ali, 2001 - period of detention to be considered in a particular context); BNSS provides that set-off does not apply to imprisonment in default of fine unless so ordered.

Mercy petition (s.472 BNSS; new; formerly governed by prison manuals): a convict sentenced to death may submit a mercy petition to the Governor within thirty days from the date on which the Superintendent of the jail informs him of the dismissal of his appeal/SLP/review, and if the Governor rejects it, to the President within sixty days from the date of the Governor's decision; where there are multiple convicts in the same case, mercy petitions must be filed by all within sixty days, and the President decides on all together; the decision of the President is final and not subject to appeal or judicial review on the merits [VERIFY the periods]. Judicial review of mercy decisions: Epuru Sudhakar v. Government of A.P. (2006); Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India (2014) - inordinate delay can commute; Kehar Singh v. Union of India (1989).

Power to suspend or remit sentences (s.473 BNSS; s.432 CrPC): the appropriate Government may suspend the execution of a sentence or remit the whole or any part of the punishment, with or without conditions; the Government may ask the presiding Judge of the convicting/confirming court for his opinion; the person must not be released if conditions are not fulfilled; the Governor's constitutional power under Art 161 is independent (Maru Ram v. Union of India, 1980). BNSS adds that a sentence of death may be commuted only to imprisonment for life; a sentence of life imprisonment only to imprisonment of not less than seven years; and imprisonment of seven years or more to imprisonment of not less than three years; the fine only may be remitted [VERIFY exact lines].

Power to commute sentence (s.474; s.433 CrPC): the appropriate Government may commute a death sentence to life imprisonment or any other term; life imprisonment to a term not exceeding fourteen years or fine; rigorous to simple imprisonment; fine to imprisonment... Restriction on powers of remission or commutation in certain cases (s.475 BNSS; s.433A CrPC): where a sentence of imprisonment for life has been imposed on conviction of an offence for which death is one of the punishments provided by law, or a death sentence has been commuted to life, the person shall not be released unless he has served at least fourteen years of imprisonment. Concurrent power of Central Government in respect of death sentences (s.476; s.434); State Government to act in consultation with the Central Government in cases investigated by a Central agency (s.477; s.435).

Remission jurisprudence: Laxman Naskar v. Union of India (2000) - factors for premature release; Union of India v. V. Sriharan (2016) - life sentence means life subject to remission by the appropriate Government after 14 years; fixed term by court; Joseph v. State of Kerala (2023) - policy-based remission; Bilkis Yakub Rasool v. Union of India (8 Jan 2024) - the 'appropriate Government' for remission is the State in which the offender was tried and sentenced, i.e., Maharashtra, not Gujarat where the offence occurred; remission orders for the 11 convicts quashed; Rashidul Jafar @ Chotu v. State of U.P. (2022) - remission must be considered even if no application is made, where a policy exists; A.G. Perarivalan v. State of Tamil Nadu (2022) - Art 142 used for release after the Governor's delay.
Suspension of sentences: s.430; Parole and furlough are governed by prison laws, not the BNSS.

sections.title: Bail and Bonds: Regular, Anticipatory, Default and Undertrial Release; Cancellation
sections.overview: Highest-yield cluster with the most case law. Know bailable v. non-bailable, anticipatory bail principles, default bail and the new s.479 rule, cancellation and the bond provisions.
must_know: Bail in bailable offences (s.478 BNSS; s.436 CrPC): when a person other than one accused of a non-bailable offence is arrested or detained without warrant or appears before a court, and is prepared to give bail, he shall be released on bail, as of right; the court or officer may release him on a personal bond without sureties; if he is unable to furnish bail within one week of his arrest, he shall be deemed to be an indigent person and released on a personal bond; the right to bail may be exercised before conviction at any time; if a person fails to comply with conditions of the bond, the court may refuse bail on a subsequent occasion (s.478(3); s.436(2)).

Bail in non-bailable offences (s.480 BNSS; s.437 CrPC): bail may be granted but not if there appear reasonable grounds for believing that the person has been guilty of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life; nor if it is a cognizable offence and he has previously been convicted of an offence punishable with death, life or imprisonment for seven years or more, or has been convicted on two or more occasions of cognizable offences punishable with three years or more but less than seven years - except where the person is under sixteen years, a woman, or sick or infirm, who may be released; the court may also release in the other cases if satisfied it is in the interest of justice. Bail if, after the conclusion of the trial and before judgment, the court finds reasonable grounds for believing the accused is not guilty (s.480(6)). Where a person is accused of an offence punishable with imprisonment of seven years or more, or of offences under the chapters on offences against the body, property and public tranquillity... the court shall impose conditions: attendance, no repetition, no inducement/threat to witnesses (s.480(3); s.437(3)). Reasons for granting or refusing bail to be recorded in writing (s.480(4)). Court may direct arrest and committal for violation (s.480(5)). Narayan v. State of M.P. (2026) - the s.480(3) mandatory conditions are not engaged for offences punishable up to seven years [VERIFY].

Principles of bail: Gudikanti Narasimhulu v. Public Prosecutor (1978) - 'bail is the rule, jail the exception'; State of Rajasthan v. Balchand (1977); Sanjay Chandra v. CBI (2012) - the object of bail is to secure presence and bail is not to be refused as a punishment; Prahlad Singh Bhati v. NCT Delhi (2001) - factors (nature of accusation, severity, character of evidence, danger of absconding, likelihood of repetition, danger to witnesses); Satender Kumar Antil v. CBI (2022) - classification of offences into Categories A to D: (A) offences punishable with imprisonment up to seven years - bail as a rule (Arnesh Kumar compliance); (B) death or life imprisonment; (C) special statutes with stringent bail conditions (NDPS s.37, PMLA s.45, UAPA s.43D(5)); (D) economic offences - and directed that bail be considered promptly (Part of Govt. direction to enact a Bail Act). Ash Mohammad v. Shiv Raj Singh (2012); Siddharam Satlingappa Mhetre v. State of Maharashtra (2010). Special statutes: Union of India v. K.A. Najeeb (2021) - prolonged incarceration can override statutory restriction; NIA v. Zahoor Ahmad Shah Watali (2019) - limited scrutiny at UAPA bail; Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. Union of India (2022) - PMLA s.45 upheld; Manish Sisodia v. CBI/ED (2024) and Prem Prakash v. Union of India (2024) - bail is the rule even under PMLA after prolonged detention; K. Kavitha v. ED (2024).

Anticipatory bail (s.482 BNSS; s.438 CrPC): when any person has reason to believe that he may be arrested on an accusation of having committed a non-bailable offence, he may apply to the High Court or the Court of Session for a direction that in the event of arrest he shall be released on bail; the court may impose conditions: to make himself available for interrogation, not to induce/threaten witnesses, not to leave India without permission, and any other condition as in s.480(3); an interim order may be passed. s.482(4) BNSS: the section does not apply to arrests on accusations of offences under BNS s.65 (rape of a woman under sixteen/twelve years) and s.70(2) (gang rape of a woman under eighteen years) - (CrPC s.438(4) bar covered IPC ss.376(3), 376AB, 376DA, 376DB) [VERIFY the BNS section mapping]. The presence of the applicant at the final hearing (s.438(1B) of the 2005 Amendment) was never brought into force.

Anticipatory bail jurisprudence: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia v. State of Punjab (1980, Constitution Bench) - anticipatory bail is not an unfettered right, courts must not impose rigid restrictions; not limited to a fixed period; not confined to exceptional cases; Sushila Aggarwal v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2020, Constitution Bench) - protection need not be limited in time and may continue till the end of trial, unless the court finds special reasons; the court may impose appropriate conditions; Siddharam Mhetre (2010) - the factors; Prathvi Raj Chauhan v. Union of India (2020) - SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act s.18/18A bars anticipatory bail unless a prima facie case is not made; Sumit v. State of U.P. (2026 INSC 145) - once granted, ordinarily continues without a fixed expiry [VERIFY details]. Concurrent jurisdiction of the Court of Session and High Court (the HC may relegate to the Sessions Court).

Special powers of the High Court or Court of Session regarding bail (s.483 BNSS; s.439 CrPC): may direct that any person accused of an offence and in custody be released on bail; may impose any condition; may set aside or modify any condition imposed by a Magistrate; notice to the PP is mandatory for offences exclusively triable by the Court of Session or punishable with life imprisonment; the informant/his authorised representative must be present at the hearing of a bail application in cases of serious sexual offences against women/children; s.483(3) (s.439(2)) - the High Court or Court of Session may direct that any person who has been released on bail under this chapter be arrested and committed to custody (cancellation). Cancellation principles: Dolat Ram v. State of Haryana (1995) - cogent and overwhelming circumstances (misuse, interference with witnesses, absconding, new offences); Mahipal v. Rajesh Kumar (2019) - cancelling an order granting bail on the ground of perversity differs from cancelling because of post-bail conduct; Neeru Yadav v. State of U.P. (2016); Abdul Basit v. Mohd. Abdul Kadir Chaudhary (2014).

Bail to require accused to appear before the next appellate court (s.481 BNSS; s.437A CrPC): before conclusion of the trial and before disposal of the appeal, the accused shall be required to execute bail bonds with sureties to appear before the higher court if an appeal or petition is filed against the judgment, for six months.

Default bail (s.187(3) BNSS; s.167(2) CrPC): see Section 2.7: indefeasible right when the investigation is not completed within 60/90 days; the right accrues the moment the period expires and application is made; Rakesh Kumar Paul (2017); M. Ravindran (2021); Bikramjit Singh (2020); Ritu Chhabaria (2023).

Release of undertrial prisoners (s.479 BNSS; s.436A CrPC): where a person has, during the period of investigation, inquiry or trial, undergone detention for a period extending up to one-half of the maximum period of imprisonment specified for that offence, he shall be released on bail by the court on his personal bond with or without sureties; BNSS (new proviso): a first-time offender (a person who has never been convicted of any offence in the past) shall be released on bail after having undergone detention for a period extending up to one-third of the maximum period; the section does not apply to offences punishable with death or life imprisonment and to persons against whom proceedings are pending in more than one offence or case; the time for delay caused by the accused is excluded; the jail Superintendent must apply in writing to the court when the accused completes the period. Bhim Singh v. Union of India (2015) - directions to apply s.436A; In Re: Inhuman Conditions in 1382 Prisons (Aug 2024) - s.479 BNSS applies to all pending cases irrespective of the date of offence/ FIR [VERIFY].

Bonds (ss.484-496 BNSS; ss.440-450 CrPC): the amount of every bond shall be fixed with due regard to the circumstances and shall not be excessive (s.484; s.440 - Moti Ram v. State of M.P., 1978; Hussainara); bond of accused and sureties (s.485; s.441); declaration by sureties (s.486; s.441A); discharge from custody (s.487; s.442); power to order sufficient bail when that first taken is insufficient (s.488; s.443); discharge of sureties (s.489; s.444); deposit instead of recognizance (s.490; s.445); procedure when bond is forfeited (s.491; s.446) - the court records the proof of forfeiture and calls upon the person to pay the penalty; cancellation of bond and bail bond (s.492; s.446A); procedure in case of insolvency/death of surety or when a bond is forfeited (s.493; s.447); bond required from minor (s.494; s.448); appeal from orders under s.491 (s.495; s.449); power to direct levy of amount due on certain recognizances (s.496; s.450).

Practical points: Bail may be denied for risk of absconding or tampering; refusal of bail by a Magistrate can be challenged in the Sessions Court/HC (concurrent), no revision is available against a bail order; bail orders must be reasoned (Brij Nandan Jaiswal v. Munna @ Munna Jaiswal, 2009; Ajwar v. Waseem, 2024 - unreasoned bail orders are set aside); no mechanical cash bail conditions (Moti Ram).

sections.title: Disposal of Property, Irregular Proceedings, Limitation, Inherent Powers, Electronic Mode and Miscellaneous
sections.overview: Custody and disposal of seized property, the effect of errors, limitation for cognizance, the High Court's inherent power (quashing), and the new electronic-mode and repeal provisions.
must_know: Order for custody and disposal of property pending trial (s.497 BNSS; s.451 CrPC): where any property is produced before a court during an inquiry or trial, the court may make such order as it thinks fit for its proper custody pending conclusion; if the property is subject to speedy and natural decay, it may be sold; BNSS (new, per press): the court must ensure that the property is photographed/videographed and a statement prepared and, after the identification/photography, the property can be released or disposed of within thirty days [VERIFY]. Sunderbhai Ambalal Desai v. State of Gujarat (2002) - valuable articles and vehicles should not be allowed to rust in police stations; release on superdari; General Insurance Council v. State of A.P. (2010). Order for disposal at the conclusion of the trial (s.498; s.452): destruction, confiscation or delivery to the person entitled; payment to an innocent purchaser (s.499; s.453); appeal against orders (s.500; s.454); stay of order (s.501; s.455); restoration of possession of immovable property after conviction for criminal force (s.502; s.456); procedure by police upon seizure of property (s.503; s.457) - report to Magistrate, order for disposal; procedure when no claimant (s.504; s.458); power to sell perishable property (s.505; s.459).

Irregular proceedings: irregularities which do not vitiate proceedings (s.506 BNSS; s.460 CrPC) - e.g., a Magistrate not empowered who erroneously takes cognizance of certain offences, issues a search warrant, tries an offender summarily, etc.; irregularities which vitiate (s.507; s.461) - e.g., attachment of property by a non-empowered Magistrate, trial of an offender by a Magistrate not empowered, taking cognizance without empowerment; proceedings in wrong place (s.508; s.462); non-compliance with confession-recording provisions (s.509; s.463) - the court may take evidence to prove that the statement was voluntary; effect of omission to frame, or absence of, or error in, charge (s.510; s.464); finding or sentence when reversible by reason of error, omission or irregularity (s.511; s.465) - not reversed unless failure of justice has in fact been occasioned; objection must be raised at the earliest (Shamnsaheb M. Multtani v. State of Karnataka, 2001); defect or error in a charge (s.512-513; ss.466-467).

Limitation for taking cognizance (s.514 BNSS; s.468 CrPC): six months - offence punishable with fine only; one year - imprisonment not exceeding one year; three years - imprisonment exceeding one year but not three years; the period is computed from the date of the offence or when it came to the knowledge of the person aggrieved or the police (s.515; s.469); exclusion of time spent diligently in another court or the period of stay (s.516; s.470); exclusion of the date on which the court is closed (s.517; s.471); continuing offences - fresh period at every moment (s.518; s.472); extension where the court is satisfied that the delay has been properly explained or that it is necessary to do so in the interests of justice (s.519; s.473). No limitation for offences punishable with more than three years. Sarah Mathew (2014); Japani Sahoo v. Chandra Sekhar Mohanty (2007); State of Punjab v. Sarwan Singh (1981).

Inherent powers of the High Court (s.528 BNSS; s.482 CrPC): nothing in the Sanhita limits or affects the inherent powers of the High Court to make such orders as may be necessary to give effect to any order under the Sanhita, or to prevent abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice. Not a source of new power; cannot override express provision; used sparingly, e.g., to quash FIR/complaint/proceedings; Bhajan Lal categories: (1) allegations taken at face value do not constitute any offence; (2) FIR and other materials do not disclose a cognizable offence justifying investigation without a Magistrate's order; (3) uncontroverted allegations and evidence collected do not disclose commission of an offence; (4) allegations disclose only a non-cognizable offence and no investigation is permitted without a Magistrate's order; (5) allegations are so absurd and inherently improbable that no prudent person could reach a conclusion; (6) express legal bar in the Code or other statute; (7) the proceeding is manifestly attended with mala fides or instituted maliciously to wreak vengeance. Cases: R.P. Kapur v. State of Punjab (1960); Neeharika Infrastructure v. State of Maharashtra (2021); Rajiv Thapar v. Madan Lal Kapoor (2013) - 'sterling' defence material; Parbatbhai Aahir (2017); Gian Singh (2012); State of M.P. v. Laxmi Narayan (2019); Mohammad Wajid v. State of U.P. (2023) - the HC should not ignore the allegations of mala fides. Quashing does not apply to heinous offences on compromise; the HC may use s.528 to give interim stay but cannot stop investigation in a routine manner.

Trial and proceedings in electronic mode (s.530 BNSS; new): all trials, inquiries and proceedings under the Sanhita, including issuance, service and execution of summons and warrants; examination of the complainant and witnesses; recording of evidence in inquiries and trials; all appellate proceedings or other proceedings, may be held in electronic mode, by use of electronic communication or audio-video electronic means. Also provides for electronic filing of the chargesheet and submission of documents; use of video-conferencing for production of prisoners; the High Court makes rules. e-Courts mission and e-Sakshya, e-Sign, MedLEaPR, e-Prisons platforms are the implementing tools [VERIFY].
Repeal and savings (s.531 BNSS): the CrPC 1973 is repealed; the Chapters of the CrPC are replaced; s.531(2): pending matters are governed by the CrPC. Section 528: High Court's inherent powers.

Other miscellaneous provisions: Criminal Procedure (Identification) Act, 2022 (replaced the Identification of Prisoners Act 1920): permits taking of measurements - fingerprints, palm-prints, footprints, photographs, iris and retina scans, physical and biological samples and behavioural attributes - of convicts and of persons arrested; records retained for 75 years; [cross-ref Related Topics].

latest_developments.topic: BNSS in force since 1 July 2024: transition and early judicial treatment
latest_developments.summary: The BNSS, BNS and BSA replaced the CrPC, IPC and Evidence Act. Offences before 1 July 2024 are tried under the IPC but proceedings begun afterwards follow BNSS procedure; pending matters continue under CrPC (s.531(2)). Courts have repeatedly applied the principle that procedural law operates prospectively from commencement while Art 20(1) protects accused against retrospective penal provisions.

latest_developments.topic: Written grounds of arrest are mandatory in every case
latest_developments.date: Mihir Rajesh Shah v. State of Maharashtra, 6 Nov 2025 (2025 INSC 1288); earlier Vihaan Kumar v. State of Haryana (Feb 2025)
latest_developments.summary: Grounds of arrest must be conveyed in writing, in a language the arrestee understands, under every statute (IPC/BNS and special laws alike); if oral intimation is made at the time of arrest, the written grounds must follow within a reasonable time and at least two hours before production before the Magistrate for remand; non-compliance renders arrest and remand illegal and entitles the person to release (without prejudice to re-arrest by compliant process). A later Supreme Court order (Sept 2026, Jaskaran Jeet Singh Deol v. State of Punjab) was reported to address the consequences of non-compliance [VERIFY].

latest_developments.likely_question: Written grounds of arrest must be furnished how long before the remand hearing? (At least two hours)

latest_developments.topic: Section 175(3) and (4) BNSS - Magistrate's power to order investigation
latest_developments.date: Supreme Court rulings Jan 2026, Apr 2026, Oct 2026 [VERIFY titles]
latest_developments.summary: The Court has examined the new conditions in s.175(3) (affidavit, inquiry, hearing the police) and s.175(4) (report from superior officer and hearing the public servant before a Magistrate directs investigation into complaints against public servants for acts in official duty). Reported holdings: s.175(4) works with s.175(3) and does not stand alone; it widens safeguards for public servants compared with s.156(3) CrPC; and no prior sanction is needed merely to direct FIR registration [VERIFY].
latest_developments.why_it_matters: New wording with no CrPC equivalent.
latest_developments.likely_question: Which BNSS section corresponds to s.156(3) CrPC? (s.175(3))

State of M.P.: anticipatory bail to be granted with circumspection in serious cases [VERIFY]; Shally Mahant v. State of Punjab (9 Feb 2026): an accused who merely does not give the answers the investigating officer desires is not 'non-cooperating' [VERIFY]; Bombay High Court (2026) held the s.482(4) bar not to be absolute in all circumstances [VERIFY].

latest_developments.summary: The Supreme Court in the prison conditions matter directed that s.479 BNSS applies to all pending cases irrespective of when the offence was committed and that jail superintendents must move the court on completion of the relevant period; first-time offenders get relief at one-third and others at one-half of the maximum term [VERIFY order date].

latest_developments.topic: Forensic investigation, e-FIR, audio-video recording: implementation
latest_developments.summary: Mandatory forensic visits for 7+ year offences (s.176(3)), audio-video recording of searches (s.105), e-FIR and electronic summons are being rolled out in phases by the States; the Home Ministry and the National Forensic Sciences University have run training programmes.
